ABSTRACT
This thesis investigates the impacts of climate change, specifically extreme events such as floods
and heatwaves, on the utilization of maternal and child health (MCH) services. Grounded in an
interdisciplinary approach that integrates realist-informed evidence synthesis, systems thinking,
and quantitative causal inference, the study is structured into three complementary essays.Essay
1consists of a realist-informed systematic review aimed at understanding whether, how, and
in which contexts extreme events affect MCH service utilization. A total of 36 quantitative
and qualitative studies were included and assessed in terms of methodological quality, type
of climatic event, study design, and geographic context. The findings indicate that floods and
heatwaves negatively affect access to antenatal, delivery, and postnatal care, particularly in
socioeconomically vulnerable settings.Essay 2employs Causal Loop Diagrams (CLDs) to
map, based on the evidence synthesized in Essay 1, the mechanisms through which floods
undermine MCH service utilization. Six core mechanisms were identified: travel capacity,
displacement, income loss, health risks, service provision, and broader infrastructure disruptions.
The qualitatively constructed CLD comprises 18 interconnected components organized into
reinforcing and balancing feedback loops, providing an integrated representation of the dynamic
interactionsbetweenhealthsystemsandclimateshocks.Essay3appliescausalinferencemethods
to estimate the effects of the 2010 floods on antenatal care utilization in the states of Pernambuco
and Alagoas, using SINASC data from 2008 to 2012. The results indicate that the main impact
of the event was not an increase in exclusion from antenatal care, but rather a reallocation in the
intensity of care. We observe a significant reduction in the proportion of women with seven or
more visits and an increase in the intermediate category (4–6 visits), with no evidence of growth
in the proportion of women with no or few visits. These findings suggest a partial disruption in
continuity of care, rather than a collapse in access to antenatal services. The methodological
complementarity across the essays strengthens the internal coherence of the thesis: Essay 1
provides the theoretical and empirical foundation for the causal mapping in Essay 2, while Essay
3 empirically tests the mechanisms identified. Taken together, the three essays demonstrate that
extreme events exacerbate pre-existing vulnerabilities and compromise continuity of care in
MCH services. The thesis advances the literature by proposing an integrated framework that
combines qualitative evidence, systems modeling, and quantitative causal analysis to inform
more resilient and equitable public policies in the context of climate change.
Keywords: Climate Change. Floods. Heatwaves. Maternal and Child Health. Interrupted Time
Series. Causal Loop Diagrams. Realist Systematic Review.

RESUMO
Esta tese investiga os impactos das mudanças climáticas, especificamente de eventos extremos
como enchentes e ondas de calor, sobre a utilização dos serviços de saúde materno-infantil
(SMI). Com base em uma perspectiva interdisciplinar que integra avaliação realista, pensamento
sistêmico e métodos quantitativos, o trabalho está estruturado em três ensaios complementares.
OEnsaio 1consiste em uma revisão sistemática realista-informada que busca compreender se,
como e em que contextos eventos extremos afetam a utilização dos serviços de SMI. Foram
incluídos 36 estudos quantitativos e qualitativos, analisados quanto à qualidade metodológica,
tipo de evento, desenho de estudo e contexto geográfico. Os resultados indicam que as enchentes
e ondas de calor afetam negativamente o acesso ao pré-natal, parto e pós-natal, principalmente
em contextos de vulnerabilidade socioeconômica. OEnsaio 2utiliza diagramas de loops causais
(CLDs) para mapear, com base na evidência sintetizada no Ensaio 1, os mecanismos pelos quais
enchentes comprometem a utilização dos serviços de SMI. Foram identificados seis mecanismos
principais:capacidadedeviajar,desalojamento,perdaderenda,riscosàsaúde,ofertadeserviços
einfraestruturaemgeral.OCLDconstruídoqualitativamentereúne18componentesorganizados
em loops de retroalimentação, oferecendo uma visão integrada das relações dinâmicas entre
sistemas de saúde e choques climáticos. OEnsaio 3aplica uma análise de inferência causal
para avaliar os efeitos das enchentes de 2010 sobre a realização de consultas de pré-natal em
Pernambuco e Alagoas, utilizando dados do SINASC entre 2008 e 2012. Os resultados revelam
que o principal impacto do evento não foi o aumento da exclusão do pré-natal, mas sim uma
realocação na intensidade do cuidado. Observou-se uma redução significativa na proporção de
mulheres com sete ou mais consultas e um aumento na categoria intermediária (4–6 consultas),
sem evidência de crescimento na proporção de mulheres com nenhuma ou poucas consultas.
Esses achados sugerem uma interrupção parcial da continuidade do cuidado, e não um colapso
no acesso ao pré-natal. A complementaridade metodológica entre os ensaios reforça a coesão da
tese: o Ensaio 1 fundamenta teoricamente o mapeamento causal do Ensaio 2, enquanto o Ensaio
3 testa empiricamente os mecanismos identificados. Em conjunto, os três ensaios evidenciam
que eventos extremos agravam vulnerabilidades existentes e comprometem a continuidade do
cuidado em SMI. A tese contribui para o avanço do conhecimento ao propor uma abordagem
integrada que combina evidência qualitativa, modelagem sistêmica e análise quantitativa para
informar políticas públicas mais resilientes e equitativas frente às mudanças climáticas.

1 INTRODUCTION
Climate change refers to long-term alterations in the state of the climate, identified by
statistically significant changes in average conditions and/or their variability over time (typically
assessedoveraminimumperiodof30years)(IntergovernmentalPanelonClimateChange,2018).
This encompasses shifts in surface temperature, precipitation patterns, wind, humidity, cloud
cover, solar radiation (insolation), atmospheric pressure, the frequency and intensity of extreme
events (e.g., hurricanes, droughts, floods, heatwaves), ice and snow cover, sea level (due to
thermal expansion and glacier melt), and greenhouse gas concentrations (World Meteorological
Organization, 2025). While the climate of Earth has always varied naturally, the current changes
are largely driven by human activities (especially the combustion of fossil fuels, deforestation,
and other land-use changes such as large-scale agriculture, pasture expansion, urbanization,
wetlanddrainage,slash-and-burnpractices,infrastructuredevelopment,andforestfragmentation)
that have increased the concentrations of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere (Roy et al., 2022).
Extreme weather events (EWEs) are meteorological occurrences that deviate markedly
from a region’s typical weather patterns in terms of intensity, duration, or spatial extent, and
usuallylieinthefartailofthehistoricaldistribution.Statistically,theseeventsareoftendefinedas
those that occur in the highest or lowest percentile of observations. Examples include heatwaves,
heavy rainfall events, floods, droughts, tropical cyclones, and severe storms. As the climate
warms, the atmosphere’s capacity to hold moisture increases and altered circulation patterns
can lead to more frequent and intense extreme events. This means that events which were once
considered “improbable” are becoming more common, contributing to higher risks of damage to
ecosystems, infrastructure, and human lives (Seneviratne et al., 2021).
Maternal and child health (MCH) systems are comprehensive networks of services,
policies, and resources designed to promote the health and well-being of women throughout
pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period, as well as to ensure the healthy growth
and development of infants and children. These systems encompass a continuum of care that
includes preconception counseling, antenatal care (such as regular health check-ups, nutritional
support, and screening for complications), skilled attendance during labor and delivery, and
postnatal services for both the mother and child. In addition, MCH systems integrate preventive
interventions like immunizations, growth monitoring, nutrition programs, and health education
initiatives that target both mothers and children. For instance, an effective MCH system might
involvecommunityhealthworkersprovidingoutreachinruralareas,primarycareclinicsoffering
routine antenatal services, and referral networks that link to higher-level facilities for emergency
obstetric care. This integrated approach is crucial for reducing maternal, newborn, and child
morbidity and mortality, a priority highlighted by the World Health Organization (WHO) in its
Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s and Adolescents’ Health (World Health Organization,
2015).

17
This thesis explores the intersection of climate change, EWEs and MCH systems through
three complementary essays. The first essay is a realist-informed systematic review examining
how heat waves and floods affect MCH systems globally. It synthesizes current evidence globally
and identifies research gaps. Building on these findings, the second essay employs a causal
loop diagram (CLD) to map the theoretical framework and illustrate how floods influence MCH
utilization. The third essay uses interrupted time series and panel data analyses to assess the
impact of floods on prenatal health service use in Pernambuco, Brazil. Each essay is original
in nature and contributes uniquely to understanding the relationship between climate extremes
and MCH. The primary goal of this thesis is to enhance our understanding of how shifting
climate patterns and extreme weather events impact maternal and child health system indicators
across diverse contexts, thereby providing critical insights to inform the development of targeted
mitigation and adaptation strategies. The three essays outlined here share a solid theoretical and
empirical foundation based on frontier research in public health (Romanello et al., 2025; Masters
et al., 2025) and health economics (Borghi e Kuhn, 2024; Hensher, 2023).
1.1 STYLIZED FACTS
Before delving deeper into any theories and models, it is imperative to shed light on
some stylized facts. Stylized facts are simplified, general empirical observations that capture
robust, recurring patterns in data across different contexts or time periods. They are not precise
in every individual instance but rather describe the broad regularities that hold on average, and
these regularities serve as benchmarks for developing, testing, and refining theoretical models.
These empirical patterns not only characterize the core of the problem but also provide the solid
foundation from which all subsequent development will unfold (Kaldor, 1961; Hirschman, 2016).

1.1.4 Climate change is considered the greatest threat to human health in the 21st century
Long-term changes in temperature, precipitation, wind, and other weather measures have

and 2050 from malnutrition, malaria, diarrhea, and heat stress, with direct health costs estimated

years, there has been growing recognition of the significant impact of climate change on human
health, with research focusing on understanding the interaction between climate change and
public health, aiming to enhance resilience and reduce risks (Romanello et al., 2025; Myhre et
al., 2025; Golden et al., 2025).

Systematic literature reviews suggest that women may be at greater risk of complications

2017; Chersich et al., 2020; Rocque et al., 2021). In addition, its indirect effects such as infras-

et al., 2021; Wheeler et al., 2022). Women in resource-poor nations, already disproportionately
affected by poverty, malnutrition, and limited education, comprise most displaced persons and
face heightened risks during disasters, as strained healthcare systems with inadequate facilities
and emergency resources further compromise prenatal care, safe delivery, and maternal-infant
health outcomes (Nour, 2011; Pappas, Kovats e Ranganathan, 2024).
Despite these concerns, pregnant women and children are frequently overlooked as a
vulnerable group in climate change research and policy discussions. Their specific needs receive
limited attention, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, where constrained funding
and other resource limitations hinder rigorous investigation into climate-related maternal–child
health outcomes (Helldén et al., 2021; Amekpor et al., 2025; Zangerl et al., 2024; Persson et al.,
2025). Many pregnant women in low- and middle-income countries live in large urban slums
or remote rural areas, the environments in which they will raise their children, and will be
increasingly subject to EWEs in the coming years (Food and Agriculture Organization of the
United Nations, 2024; Bhanbhro e Ali, 2025).
1.2 A HEALTH ECONOMICS PERSPECTIVE ON CLIMATE IMPACTS: EVIDENCE
FROM BRAZIL
Despite increasing global attention to climate impacts on health, empirical research on
climate extremes and maternal–child health outcomes in Brazil remains limited. Early work in
health economics examined climatic determinants of infant mortality: Rosenberg et al. (2000)
used ordinary least squares (OLS) regression to assess the effects of temperature, precipitation,
altitude, and coastal proximity on infant mortality across all Brazilian municipalities in 1996.
Pereda, Menezes e Alves (2014) found, through panel data econometrics, that both excessive
and insufficient rainfall increase neonatal mortality rates and the incidence of low birth weight
in Brazilian states. Using the same method, Rocha e Soares (2015) found that water scarcity
(lack of rainfall) in municipalities in Brazil’s semi-arid region is strongly correlated with higher
infant mortality, lower birth weight, and shorter gestation periods. Mata et al. (2023) examined a
large-scale adaptation intervention in Brazil’s semi-arid region, showing that access to cisterns
improved birth outcomes, underscoring the role of resilience interventions in mitigating climatic
stressors.
Morerecentobservationalevidencestrengthensthecaseforclimateimpactsonpregnancy
outcomes. In a nationally representative study of nearly 10 million live births, Requia e
Papatheodorou(2024)foundthatambienttemperatureexposureduringpregnancywasassociated
withincreasedriskofpretermbirthacrossmultipleregionsofBrazil,particularlyintheNorthand
Midwest, indicating that heat exposure may provoke earlier labor and regionally heterogeneous
vulnerability patterns. Complementing this, Feldens e Oliveira (2026) uses nearly 45 million
births across Brazilian municipalities (2000–2020) to demonstrate that temperature extremes and
deviations from historical weather patterns significantly reduce birth weight, with the strongest
effects in isolated and underserved areas and during the third trimester. Parfitt e Goulart (2026),

27
using administrative data on 25 million births in Brazilian public hospitals (2008–2019), shows
that extreme heat also affects the organization of care within maternity wards, reducing overall
cesarean rates, shifting deliveries from physicians to nurses, and increasing pre-labor cesareans
among physician-led births. Together, these findings point to intertwined physiological stress
responses and operational health system adjustments as distinct yet complementary mechanisms
of maternal–child climate vulnerability in Brazil.
Animportantfeatureofthisemergingliteratureistheapplicationofeconometricmethods
to identify causal effects of climate variability on health outcomes. Economists frequently
conceptualize extreme weather events as exogenous shocks (quasi-natural experiments) that
generate plausibly random variation in exposure across time and space. By exploiting high-
frequency climate data combined with administrative health records, researchers are able to
implement fixed-effects models, difference-in-differences strategies, and other causal inference
techniques to isolate the impact of temperature spikes, rainfall anomalies, or floods on health
service utilization and birth outcomes. This framework has been successfully applied in other
contexts to link climate shocks to disruptions in maternal and child health service use (Haque,
Parr e Muhidin, 2020a; Haque, Parr e Muhidin, 2020b; Chandir et al., 2023), demonstrating how
environmental stressors can alter both demand-side behavior and supply-side constraints within
health systems.
From a health economics standpoint, the proposed topic is both timely and relevant.

period is a valuable form of human capital , since children who are healthy from birth live longer,
attain higher levels of education, become more productive adults, and earn higher wages in the
future (Currie, 2020; Carrets, 2021). Maternal health interventions have proven effectiveness
and cost-effectiveness, as they not only save mothers’ lives but also reduce neonatal mortality
and morbidity, help combat inequality and improve the overall performance of health systems
(Borghi et al., 2006). Furthermore, it is suggested that improvements in child and maternal health
may generate positive economic benefits for gross domestic product (GDP) per capita, especially
in developing countries (Trondillo, 2016; Klobodu et al., 2019).
Climatechangeandextremeweathereventsposeamultifacetedchallengetomaternaland
child health service utilization, and economic theory and methods provide a coherent framework
to understand and address this challenge. By viewing healthcare as a system where providers
supply services and families demand care, we can identify how climate shocks alter incentives,
constraints, and outcomes. Supply represents the healthcare system’s capacity to provide services
such as hospitals, clinics, medical personnel, equipment, and medications. Demand represents
the need and willingness of individuals to seek and use those services, influenced by factors
like perceived benefits, costs (monetary and non-monetary), and accessibility. Even though
healthcare often isn’t a classical market (many services are subsidized or free at point of use), the
core principles still apply. Utilization will be high when services are readily available (ample
supply) and people are able and willing to access care (strong demand). Conversely, if supply is

28
constrained or demand is suppressed, utilization falls. Importantly, climate change and extreme
weather events can act as shocks to either side of this equation, upsetting the balance. By
examining how supply-side constraints (like damaged infrastructure and strained resources) and
demand-side barriers (like reduced access and altered priorities) coincide during climate events,
we uncover the mechanisms, analogous to shifts in supply and demand, behind observed drops in
service use.
The economic perspective is not just an academic exercise; it has practical and political
implications. It directs us to ask: How can we relax the supply constraints (perhaps through
resilient design and surge staffing)? How can we lower the barriers on the demand side (perhaps
through mobile clinics, transport, or emergency cash support)? The global nature of climate
change means these questions are relevant from Bangladesh to Brazil, even as local context
modifies specifics. In Brazil’s case, we see that a strong public health system alone is not enough.
Resilience against climate shocks must be built through smart investments and policies (Golden
et al., 2025), many of which boil down to allocating resources efficiently under uncertainty.
In the language of economics, it means moving the supply and demand curves in the right
direction through investment, incentives, and innovation so that the equilibrium level of MCH
service utilization remains high, safeguarding maternal and child health in a changing climate.
This is where evidence-based public policies become essential, as they must be designed and
implementedonthebasisofrigorousdata,scientificanalysis,andempiricalevaluationratherthan
intuition or political convenience. By grounding decisions in robust evidence, policymakers can
more effectively target resources, anticipate unintended consequences, and design interventions
thatarenotonlycost-effectivebutalsoequitableandcontextuallyappropriate,whichisespecially
critical in the face of complex and evolving climate-health challenges (Hess et al., 2014).

2 REALIST-INFORMED SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
ABSTRACT
Background:Heatwaves and floods are increasing globally, posing risks to healthcare
systems and disrupting maternal and child health (MCH) service utilisation. Understanding
whether, how, and in which contexts floods and heatwaves affect MCH is essential for effective
adaptation planning.
Methods:We conducted a realist-informed systematic review across seven databases,
identifying 5,280 records. After dual screening, 36 studies met inclusion criteria, reporting the
effects of floods and/or heatwaves on routine and emergency MCH service utilisation (23 floods,
12heatwaves,1both).Norestrictionswereappliedbylanguage,setting,orstudydesign.Findings
were synthesised narratively.
Results:Evidence for heatwaves is stronger for emergency and inpatient care, including
maternal hospitalisations, obstetric emergencies, neonatal intensive care admissions, and under-
five emergency department visits, while evidence on routine care is very limited. In contrast,
floodsareassociatedwithreducedroutineservices,includingantenatalcare,institutionaldelivery,
and postnatal care; floods also impede access to emergency obstetric care, leading to delayed
referrals and preventable deaths.
Conclusion:Floods and heatwaves affect MCH service utilisation through shared and
hazard-specific pathways shaped by contextual vulnerability. Key gaps remain, including limited
qualitative evidence on heatwaves, scarce research on child health services beyond acute care,
and uneven geographic coverage. These findings can inform targeted strategies to strengthen
climate-resilient MCH systems.

2.1 INTRODUCTION
The objective of this essay is to explore whether, how, and in which contexts heatwaves
andfloodsaffecttheutilizationofmaternalandchildhealthcareservices.Bymappingthecurrent
evidence, identifying key pathways, and emphasizing the contextual variability of these effects,
this review seeks to inform future policies and interventions to mitigate the adverse economic
and human capital impacts associated with climate-induced disruptions in maternal and child
healthcare.
A heatwave refers to a period during which an area experiences excessive and prolonged
heat, marked by several unusually hot days in a row. These events involve persistently high
maximum and minimum temperatures, which may extend from a few days to even months,
depending on the region. Both daytime and nighttime temperatures are critical because when
nights remain hot, the body has less chance to recover, and extreme temperatures tend to occur
earlier in the day and persist for longer periods (World Meteorological Organization, 2026a).
Floods are natural disasters that occur when an overflow of water submerges land that
is usually dry. The three most common types of floods are flash floods (caused by rapid, heavy
rainfall), river floods (caused by prolonged rain or snowmelt overflowing rivers), and coastal
floods (caused by storm surges or tsunamis) (World Meteorological Organization, 2026b).
Examples of service utilization for mothers and women of reproductive age include
antenatal check-ups, institutional delivery care (for normal and complicated births), postnatal
follow-up visits, and family planning services. Care for newborns and children under five years
comprises routine health screening, essential nutrition services, and regular vaccinations. Thus,
MCH utilization is the extent to which healthcare services designed to improve the health
outcomes of mothers and children are accessed and used by the target population (Sarikhani,
Najibi e Razavi, 2024).
The intersection of climate factors and human health has gained prominence in recent
years,promptingameticulousexaminationofhowthesechangesaffectvulnerablegroups(World

at risk because of their heightened physiological and developmental vulnerabilities (Rylander,
Odland e Sandanger, 2013; Kuehn e McCormick, 2017; Roos et al., 2021), which amplify both
direct and indirect health consequences during extreme weather events.
The impacts of adverse shocks in early childhood include an increased likelihood of
developing chronic illnesses (such as diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular diseases),
greater incidence of mental health disorders (like depression and anxiety), reduced cognitive
performance, physical limitations, and a higher risk of premature mortality in adulthood (Carrets,
2021). Exposure to environmental shocks during early childhood (from the prenatal period
through age five) can lead to long-lasting and potentially irreversible impacts across the life cycle
by disrupting fetal development, impairing cognitive and physical health, reducing educational
attainment, and diminishing labor market outcomes in adulthood, with effects compounded over
time through biological damage, reduced parental investment, and socioeconomic vulnerability

2.2 METHODS
This section outlines the methods used to examine how floods and heatwaves affect the
utilisation of maternal and child healthcare services. We conducted a realist-informed systematic
review that combined rigorous procedures for identifying, selecting, appraising, and extracting
evidence with a theory-driven analysis of the contexts and mechanisms shaping the observed
outcomes. The subsections describe the initial theoretical framework, search strategy, study
selection and appraisal, data extraction, and evidence synthesis.
2.2.1 Realist-informed systematic review
Conventional systematic reviews and meta-analyses excel at estimating average effects,
yet their conclusions can be unstable when effects vary across settings, populations, and health
systems. Complexity-oriented frameworks contend that policy-relevant evidence must model
interdependence, non-linearity, and context–mechanism interactions rather than merely quantify
mean effects (Rutter et al., 2017). A Realist-Informed Systematic Review (RISR) addresses this
challenge by combining the procedural rigour of systematic reviewing (transparent searching,
explicit eligibility criteria, critical appraisal) with realist logic, which asks what works, for
whom, in what contexts, through which mechanisms, and why (Pawson et al., 2005; Wong et al.,
2013; Wong et al., 2016). In practice, RISR retains systematic processes for searching, selection,
appraisal, and extraction, while structuring questions, data coding, synthesis, and reporting
around realist constructs and theory refinement. A RISR draws on scientific/critical realism1,
which assumes that social programs work (or not) through underlying causal mechanisms whose
activation depends on contexts. A Context–Mechanism–Outcome (CMO) configuration is the
basic “unit” of realist explanation: in context C, mechanism M is triggered, producing outcome
O (Pawson et al., 2005; Wong et al., 2013).
Mechanisms(M)arethegenerativecausalprocessesthatproducechangewhentriggered
in a given context. A widely used operationalisation is resources + reasoning: programmes
introduce resources (e.g., tools, opportunities, constraints) that interact with actors’ reasoning
(e.g., beliefs, norms, capabilities), yielding change. Distinguishing mechanisms from programme
1 Scientific/criticalrealismisaphilosophyofsciencewhichholdsthatamind-independentworldexists(ontological
realism). Reality is stratified into the real (underlying structures and generative mechanisms), the actual (events
those mechanisms generate), and the empirical (what we observe). Our knowledge is theory-laden and fallible
(epistemic relativism), yet we can still judge between explanations by how well they account for the evidence
across settings (judgmental rationality). See Bhaskar (1975) -A Realist Theory of Science, and Pawson e Tilley
(1997) -Realistic Evaluation, for foundational overviews.

35
activities (typically treated as part of the context) is essential for valid causal explanation (Dalkin
et al., 2015; Shaw et al., 2018).
Context(C)comprisestheconditionsthatenableorconstrainmechanisms:organisational
structures, resources, governance, incentives, professional norms, sociodemographics, place, and
timing. Context is not mere “setting”; it denotes the features that shape mechanism activation,
which may be conceived as relatively static triggers/constraints or as dynamic, relational,
multilevel processes evolving over time, two narratives with distinct implications for review
design, aims, and inference (Greenhalgh e Manzano, 2022).
Outcomes (O)are the observable consequences of mechanism activation in each context
- intended or unintended, beneficial or harmful, and occurring at proximal, intermediate, or distal
points in time. In realist synthesis, outcomes are often conceptualized as chains: early shifts (e.g.,
in actors’ reasoning or behaviour) can cumulate into later organisational or system-level effects
or be dampened when contextual features inhibit the mechanism (Pawson, 2006).
RISR seeks to build an interlocking set of CMO configurations that together constitute a
programme theory of how an intervention or phenomenon generates its effects. Reviews typically
articulate initial programme theories (IPTs) during scoping and iteratively refine them via testing,
confirmation, refutation, and elaboration into middle-range theories that “travel” across settings
while specifying boundary conditions (Pawson, 2010; Wong et al., 2013). Because mechanisms
are contingent, realist reviewers expect demi-regularities (recurrent but non-universal patterns)
rather than uniform effects, and they use these patterned regularities to strengthen explanatory
propositions (Pawson, 2006).
Realist synthesis is deliberately method-plural: instead of ranking designs, it values any
study that helps test or refine C–M–O explanations, judged on relevance and rigour. Quantitative
studies map patterns and boundaries, qualitative/process studies reveal how people reason and
which contextual features matter, and mixed-methods link the two; reviewers then weave this
evidence to compare and strengthen CMO explanations (Wong et al., 2013).
Althoughoftenpresentedlinearly,realist-informedreviewsareiterativeandtheory-driven,
usually following a six steps process (Wong, 2018; Pawson, 2006):
a) Locate existing theories to develop the IPTs (drawing on conceptual literature, prior
evaluations, and stakeholder expertise).
b) Search for data using comprehensive and purposive, theory-refining strategies (often with
an information specialist).
c) Selectdocumentsbasedonrelevance(doesthesourceinformC,M,O,orthelinksbetween
them for theory building/testing?) and rigour (are the inferences warranted given the
methods and data?).
d) Extract and organise data with templates that code for C, M (resources/ reasoning), O, and
CMO linkages; log rival mechanisms and contextual contingencies.

36
e) Analyse and synthesise using retroductive reasoning, i.e., moving between data and theory
to infer the most plausible underlying mechanisms and enabling/ constraining contexts;
adjudicate between rival CMOs on explanatory coherence and reach.
f) Test and refine programme theory into transferable middle-range theory, making explicit
the contexts under which mechanisms are likely (or unlikely) to produce desired outcomes.
This study follows the six steps for conducting an iterative realist-informed review as
described by Pawson (2006) and Wong (2018) and implemented by Borghi et al. (2018) and
Singh et al. (2021). The systematic approach follows the guideline of the Preferred Reporting
Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020), as proposed by Page et al.
(2021). The review protocol was published in PROSPERO (Silva et al., 2024).
2.2.2 Initial theoretical framework
We began by developing an initial programme theory. Based on the literature gap, we
identified two climate hazards (heat waves and floods) and one set of outcomes (utilization of
MCH services). Our initial hypothesis is that heat waves and floods disrupt the utilization of
maternalandchildhealthcare(MCH)servicesbycreatingbothsupply-anddemand-sidebarriers.
On the supply side, these events can undermine service availability (for example, infrastructure
destruction or staff shortages), while on the demand side, they can affect affordability (income
lossorincreasedout-of-pocketcosts)andacceptability(safetyconcernsornormsaroundseeking
care). Building on this understanding, we hypothesize the pathways through which exposure
to floods and heatwaves may shape MCH utilization. These pathways were identified through
discussionwithexpertsontheeffectsofflood/heateffectsonmaternalandchildhealthandhealth
systems, and constitute an initial theoretical framework.
Wehypothesizethatthesepathwaysrarelyoperateinisolation.Forinstance,displacement
and migration can reduce household income (thereby affecting affordability) while also overbur-
dening healthcare services in receiving areas and exacerbating supply-side constraints. Similarly,
damage to transportation networks limits the ability to travel for both providers and patients,
fueling a cycle in which decreased availability of care further dampens demand. Contextual
factors - such as urban or rural location, degree of remoteness, health system decentralization,
staffing and funding levels, and overall income level - further determine the severity and nature
of these disruptions.

2.2.6 Analysing and synthesing data
We assessed the methodological quality and risk of bias of the included studies using the
Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), which is specifically designed for systematic reviews
that incorporate qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods research (Hong, Gonzalez-Reyes e
Pluye,2018).Giventhesubstantialheterogeneityinstudydesigns,exposures,outcomes,contexts,
and analytical strategies, a quantitative meta-analysis was not appropriate. Instead, we employed
a narrative (descriptive) synthesis. Narrative synthesis is a well-established and recommended
approach for integrating diverse forms of evidence, as it enables the identification of recurring
patterns, underlying mechanisms, and contextual influences across studies (Popay et al., 2006).
We first categorized the studies by methodological approach (quantitative, qualitative, or
mixed-methods) and then grouped them according to the specific MCH outcomes examined (e.g.,
antenatal, delivery, and postnatal care), as well as by geographical and socioeconomic context
(urban versus rural settings and high-income versus low- and middle-income countries). We
extracted detailed methodological information, including statistical models used in quantitative
analyses (e.g., logistic regression, difference-in-differences, Poisson and segmented regression,
and distributed lag non-linear models), qualitative analysis techniques (e.g., thematic coding and
framework analysis), and integration strategies applied in mixed-methods studies. The findings
were then synthesized narratively to highlight common themes, methodological trends, and
contextual variations, thereby providing a coherent and comprehensive account of the evidence.

2.3.1 Heatwaves
Heatwaves are commonly defined as extended periods of abnormally high temperatures
lasting from several consecutive days to, in some contexts, even months, during which both
maximum and minimum temperatures substantially exceed the typical range for a given location
(World Meteorological Organization, 2026a). Importantly, however, the studies included in this
review operationalised heat exposure using markedly different definitions, many of which do
not strictly correspond to the meteorological definition of a heatwave. By definition, a “wave”
requires at least two consecutive days of elevated temperatures; under this criterion, only five
studies applied a duration-based heatwave definition (Campbell et al., 2019; Davis et al., 2020;
Smith et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2017). The remaining studies instead focused on
high-, hot-, or extreme-temperature days, rather than sustained heat events. We did not include
studies focused on isolated high temperature (non-daily measures), as these would deviate too far
from the conceptual definition of heatwaves.
Although this heterogeneity in exposure definitions is not ideal, we deliberately adopted
broader inclusion criteria to capture the full scope of evidence linking daily heat exposure to
MCH service use. Restricting inclusion to studies using strict heatwave definitions would have
resultedinanevidencebasetoolimitedtosupportmeaningfulsynthesisorinference.Temperature
metrics also varied substantially across studies: some employed absolute thresholds, while others
relied on relative, percentile-based measures; most used daily maximum or mean temperatures,
and very few incorporated minimum temperatures. This diversity shows the lack of consensus in
the literature regarding the most appropriate operationalisation of heatwave exposure, despite
existing guidance from the World Meteorological Organization (2026a).

presentationsonnon-heatwavedaysmatchedbydayofweek,month,andyear,finding19%higher
odds (OR: 1.19; 95% CI: 1.04-1.36) of ED visits among children aged 0–5 during heatwaves in
Tasmania. Similarly, Xu et al. (2014) found that ED admissions among under-5 children rose
sharply at temperatures above 27°C in Australia, with more than a threefold increase in the risk
of EDAs during heatwaves compared to moderate temperatures. In the United States, Davis et al.
(2020) observed a 20% increase in ED visits among children aged 1–4 on heatwave days (OR =
1.20;95%CI:1.05-1.37),whileStowelletal.(2023)reportedasmallbutnon-significantincrease
in heat-related ED admissions among children aged 0-5 years (OR = 1.06; 95% CI: 0.93-1.20).
Similarly, one study that looked at the impact of heat on primary care visits. Smith et al. (2016)
reported that primary care (general practitioner; GP) consultations for heat illness in children
under-5 were three times higher during the 2013 UK heatwave compared to non-heatwave years
(IRR = 3.0; 95% CI: -7.5 TO 13.5), although the overall burden of heat was low.
2.3.2 Floods
Floods are hydro-meteorological event that occurs when water overflows and submerges
land that is normally dry. The most common flood types include flash floods, caused by intense
and short-duration rainfall; riverine (fluvial) floods, resulting from rivers exceeding their channel
capacity; and coastal floods, typically driven by storm surges or tsunamis (World Meteorological
Organization, 2026b).
Across the studies reviewed, the empirical evidence is overwhelmingly concentrated on
riverine floodplain flooding, most often seasonal and monsoon-driven, reflecting the dominant
hydrological reality of many low- and middle-income settings in South Asia and sub-Saharan
Africa. Recurring riverine flooding is the primary focus for studies in Bangladesh (Abdullah et
al., 2019; Baten et al., 2020; Ray-Bennett et al., 2021; Orderud et al., 2022; Purno et al., 2023),
India (Barman, Sarif e Saha, 2023; Surekha, Anbazhagan e Kiran, 2020), Pakistan (Jacquet et
al., 2016; Sadia et al., 2016), Nigeria (Amoo et al., 2018), South Sudan (Wilunda et al., 2016;

46
Wilunda et al., 2017), Zambia (Mroz et al., 2023), Cambodia (Saulnier et al., 2020; Saulnier et
al., 2022), and Mozambique (Firoz et al., 2016; Makanga et al., 2017).
Severalstudiesemphasiseriverbankerosionasacoreelementofriverinefloodingdynam-
ics in Bangladesh, highlighting its role in land loss, displacement, and prolonged vulnerability
(Haque,ParreMuhidin,2019;Haque,ParreMuhidin,2020a;Haque,ParreMuhidin,2020b).In
contrast,onlyalimitednumberofstudiesexplicitlyaddresscompoundflooding,inwhichriverine
floods are intensified by pluvial rainfall, flash flooding, or coastal storm surges, as documented
in Pakistan (Chandir et al., 2023), northern Iran (Peyravi, Rahnavard e Marzaleh, 2020), and
coastal Bangladesh (Shah, Miller e Mothabbir, 2019). Urban pluvial flooding is particularly
underrepresented, appearing in only a single study focused on low-income urban communities in
Ghana (Codjoe et al., 2020). Moreover, this body of literature largely overlooks coastal flooding
as a standalone hazard, as well as chronic waterlogging and groundwater-driven inundation,
despite the increasing importance of these flood types under climate change and sea-level rise.
2.3.2.1 Impacts on routine care
Antenatal care (ANC) and delivery care are the most frequently reported outcomes in
the literature on floods. Floods were associated with a reduction in ANC utilisation, particularly
among displaced populations (Baten et al., 2020; Haque, Parr e Muhidin, 2020a). Repeated
displacementexposureoverrecentyears,includingbeforeorbetweenpregnancies,wasassociated
with substantially reduced ANC use, as women displaced three or more times had lower odds
of receiving any ANC (OR = 0.32; 95% CI: 0.17-0.64) and of completing four or more ANC
visits (OR = 0.38; 95% CI: 0.18-0.78), while one or two displacements showed no significant
effect (Haque, Parr e Muhidin, 2020a). However, Orderud et al. (2022) found no significant
average effects of flood exposure on antenatal or delivery care, except for a small decline in at
least one ANC visit 25–36 months post-flood (-2.1%; 95% CI: -4.2% to -0.1%). In Nigeria, ANC
coverageamongdisplacedwomenfellfrom82.4%pre-floodto53.3%post-floodduetotransport
and income loss (Amoo et al., 2018). While most studies highlight negative effects, Baten et al.
(2020) found that women in flood-affected areas were more likely to complete four or more ANC
visits(adjustedOR=1.20;95%CI:1.04–1.38),likelyreflectingmitigationthroughhumanitarian
support, but repeated flooding reduced ANC use, with women in twice-flooded areas having
substantially lower odds of adequate ANC compared with once-flooded areas (OR = 0.57; 95%
CI: 0.46–0.70). In Rumbek North (South Sudan), floods during the wet season make travel to
ANC unsafe or impossible and can disrupt supplies, so attendance drops most in remote villages
and cattle camps where distance, lack of transport, insecurity, domestic burdens, and husbands’
restrictions compound the access shock (Wilunda et al., 2017).
Across studies, floods are linked to lower rates of institutional delivery and skilled birth
attendance (Sadia et al., 2016; Baten et al., 2020; Haque, Parr e Muhidin, 2020b; Orderud et al.,
2022). In Pakistan, only 41.9% of births were attended by a skilled provider six months after the
major 2010 floods, with access especially poor for rural and low-income households (Jacquet

47
et al., 2016). In two union councils in Nowshera that were among the areas most affected by
Pakistan’s2010floods,across-sectionalhouseholdsurveyconductedinSeptember2013–January
2014 found very low maternal health service use (ANC 45%, skilled birth attendance 26%,
facilitydelivery19.7%);however,thesefiguresaredescriptiveandcannotbeattributedcausallyto
flooding, as they may also reflect pre-existing under-resourcing and socioeconomic disadvantage
(Sadia et al., 2016). In Rumbek North (South Sudan), floods during the rainy season render roads
impassable and paralyse referral systems, forcing planned facility births to revert to home or
cattle-camp deliveries and leading to reported maternal and newborn deaths when women must
be carried “on shoulders” and complications cannot be referred (Wilunda et al., 2016).

babies 18% less likely to receive newborn PNC (OR 0.82, 95% CI: 0.72-0.93); repeated floods
further worsened these odds (once- vs four-times flooded: maternal PNC OR 0.43 [0.32–0.59];
newborn PNC OR 0.41 [0.31–0.55]) (Baten et al., 2020). Among households displaced by
flooding three or more times, neonates had 63% lower odds of receiving PNC from a trained
provider (OR 0.37, 95% CI: 0.15-0.92) (Haque, Parr e Muhidin, 2020b). A national analysis for

overall once socioeconomic/demographic differences were controlled for (and did not report
PNC specifically), but subgroup analyses restricted to women who had lived 8 or more years
in the same area (to investigate whether migration could affect results) showed some negative
associations: flood exposure 25–36 months before birth was linked to lower likelihood of skilled
birth attendance (OR –0.026; 95% CI: -0.051, -0.001) and facility delivery (OR –0.032; 95% CI:
-0.059, -0.006), consistent with potential harms from specific floods in particular contexts despite
a null national-average effect (Orderud et al., 2022).
Floods can disrupt routine child health services. Childhood immunization coverage
dropped by 19% following a flood disaster in Pakistan, leading to approximately 11,500 missed
doses (Chandir et al., 2023). Treatments for childhood pneumonia and diarrhoea fell by 30%
during flood months compared to pre-flood months in rural Bangladesh due to clinic closures
and supply chain breakdowns (Shah, Miller e Mothabbir, 2019). Healthcare-seeking behaviours
is low among flood-displaced families: 15.5% of ill children received no care or only home
treatment, and among those taken for care outside the home, treatment by a trained provider was
lesscommonfordisplacedthannon-displacedchildren(10.3%vs35.0%),consistentwithalower
likelihood of using a trained provider (OR 0.44; 95% CI 0.26-0.73) (Haque, Parr e Muhidin,
2019).
Sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR), including family planning and post-

Evidence from Bangladesh suggests these gaps can be mitigated: the Reproductive Health in

while a post-2022 flood programme deploying trained midwives to remote union centres (with
supportive supervision, logistics, and community volunteers) delivered high volumes of SRHR
care and increased service delivery versus the same period in the prior year (Purno et al., 2023).

Floodswerefoundtoimpedeaccesstohospital-basedmaternalcareforemergencyobstet-

deaths during flood periods that were directly linked to flood-induced transport disruptions and
community isolation, with women dying on route to facilities due to prolonged delays caused
by reliance on boat transport and impassable roads. Flooded roads, high transportation costs,
and a lack of ambulances hindered timely referrals (Shah, Miller e Mothabbir, 2019; Peyravi,
Rahnavard e Marzaleh, 2020). Midwives played a crucial role in stabilizing emergencies and
initiating referrals (Purno et al., 2023).
2.3.3 Narrative synthesis
Across 36 included studies, floods and heatwaves disrupted MCH service utilisation
through hazard-specific pathways and context-dependent mechanisms. Evidence on extreme
heat was predominantly centred on acute care, with multiple studies reporting increases in
emergency department visits and inpatient utilisation for pregnant women and infants during
high-temperature days and heatwaves (Campbell et al., 2019; Davis et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2014;
Smith et al., 2016; Stowell et al., 2023). These patterns were most frequently documented in
urban, high-income settings, where heat island dynamics may intensify exposure and where
hospital-based administrative datasets allow timely detection of acute events (Chen et al., 2022;
Codjoe et al., 2020).
Evidence on heat impacts onroutinematernal care was limited: only one study explicitly
examined missed ANC visits and delayed care-seeking during heat events (Bishwakarma, 2022).
Across the studies that addressed care delivery constraints, facility-level conditions appeared to
shapeheat-relatedrisksandservicesafety,includinghighindoortemperatures,unreliablecooling
or power supply, and overcrowding affecting obstetric and neonatal care (Kakkad et al., 2014;
Codjoe et al., 2020). Household resources and social stratification also conditioned vulnerability,
including unequal access to cooling and patterns of racial and socioeconomic disadvantage in
exposure and care-seeking (Cil e Kim, 2022; Kim, Lee e Rossin-Slater, 2021; Chen et al., 2022).
A small subset of studies described adaptations such as heat-adapted service design, community
outreach, and aeromedical retrieval, which supported continuity of safe care in specific contexts
(Kakkad et al., 2014; Quilty et al., 2024).

49
In contrast, flood-related evidence more consistently reported reductions in routine MCH
services (particularly ANC, institutional delivery, postnatal care, and childhood immunisations)
often linked to disrupted transport networks, impaired referral pathways, and displacement
(Makanga et al., 2017; Mroz et al., 2023; Baten et al., 2020). These barriers were most acute
in rural floodplains, where sparse facility distribution and constrained mobility already limited
access (Makanga et al., 2017; Barman, Sarif e Saha, 2023). Several studies described delayed
recoveryofservicecoverageafterfloodsduetostaffshortages,supplydisruptions,andtemporary
relocations (Shah, Miller e Mothabbir, 2019; Peyravi, Rahnavard e Marzaleh, 2020; Chandir et
al., 2023). Reported adaptations included mobile clinics, redistribution of midwifery capacity,
cash transfers, service provision on higher ground, and transport solutions (boats, 4×4 vehicles,
aircraft) to mitigate delays in emergency obstetric care (Ray-Bennett et al., 2021; Purno et al.,
2023; Saulnier et al., 2022; Wilunda et al., 2016; Quilty et al., 2024).
Across both hazards, studies suggested that disruption patterns were conditioned by
baseline system capacity and social vulnerability, including differential access by socioeconomic
status, gender norms, and household resources, as well as variation in the governance and
functioning of referral pathways (Haque, Parr e Muhidin, 2019; Amoo et al., 2018; Firoz et al.,
2016; Cil e Kim, 2022; Kim, Lee e Rossin-Slater, 2021).
2.4 DISCUSSION
This realist-informed systematic review advances the literature by moving beyond
documenting associations between extreme weather events and MCH outcomes to explicitly
theorising how floods and heatwaves disrupt service utilisation through context–mechanism–
outcome (CMO) configurations. The urgency of strengthening such causal understanding is
underscored by major scientific assessments: climate change is already increasing hazardous
heat and heavy precipitation extremes, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations and
placing growing pressure on health systems (Pörtner et al., 2022; Romanello et al., 2025). Within
this risk landscape, MCH services are particularly sensitive to disruptions in mobility, facility
readiness, and household constraints, because continuity of preventive and time-sensitive care
(ANC, delivery, PNC, and immunisation) depends on functioning referral pathways, reliable
access, and trusted service delivery.
Prior reviews have demonstrated adverse effects of extreme weather on maternal health
in LMICs (Pappas, Kovats e Ranganathan, 2024) and on healthcare utilisation in rural and
remotesettings(Dewietal.,2024),buttheylargelysynthesiseoutcomesorbroadthemeswithout
systematically mapping the causal pathways that connect hazards to health system disruption. In
parallel, the heat-in-pregnancy evidence base has been synthesised mainly around biomedical
outcomes (e.g., preterm birth, stillbirth, neonatal complications), including recent large-scale
meta-analytic work (Lakhoo et al., 2025) and studies focusing on early-life growth (Bonell et al.,
2024).Thesesynthesesstrengthenconfidenceinheat-relatedrisks,yettheyprovidelimitedinsight
intoservicecontinuityandsystem-leveldisruption.ReviewsofMCHservicesduringemergencies

50
and disasters often aggregate heterogeneous shocks (pandemics, conflicts, and natural hazards)
and therefore tend not to distinguish hazard-specific mechanisms or the conditions under which
disruptions persist (Sahoo et al., 2021). Finally, broader syntheses of extreme weather impacts on
health services highlight that service disruption remains under-synthesised relative to individual
health outcomes (Valente et al., 2026).
Flood impacts predominantly operate through structural barriers to access and continuity:
damaged roads, disrupted transport networks, impaired referral pathways, and displacement
undermine routine care-seeking and service delivery. This mechanism profile is consistent with
the stronger and more consistent evidence of declines in ANC, institutional delivery, PNC, and
immunisation coverage observed in flood-affected settings (Makanga et al., 2017; Baten et al.,
2020; Chandir et al., 2023). Importantly, the flood pathway is not necessarily short-lived: several
studies suggest recovery lags well beyond physical repairs due to staff shortages, supply-chain
disruptions, and temporary relocation of services (Shah, Miller e Mothabbir, 2019; Peyravi,
Rahnavard e Marzaleh, 2020; Chandir et al., 2023). From a health economics perspective,
floods produce both direct constraints (physical access) and indirect constraints (income shocks,
displacement, heightened opportunity costs), which can amplify delays and increase preventable
morbidity and mortality (Haque, Parr e Muhidin, 2019; Amoo et al., 2018; Firoz et al., 2016).
In contrast, extreme heat more frequently manifests as increased acute service utilisation
via heightened maternal and neonatal risk, particularly in urban and high-income contexts where
hospital administrative data are readily available and heat island dynamics intensify exposure
(Campbell et al., 2019; Davis et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022; Codjoe et al., 2020). However, the
limited evidence on routine maternal care during heat events represents a critical blind spot. This
asymmetry likely reflects both methodological convenience (hospital datasets capturing acute
episodes) and a research emphasis on biomedical outcomes rather than continuity of primary
care. The single identified study on missed ANC during heat events suggests that, in settings
with weak transport and limited household adaptation capacity, heat may also act as a barrier to
routine care, but the current evidence base is insufficient to characterise this pathway robustly
(Bishwakarma, 2022).
Acrossbothhazards,facilityconditionsemergeasanintermediatelayershapingutilisation
and outcomes. High indoor temperatures, unreliable cooling and power, and overcrowding
compromise the delivery and safety of obstetric and neonatal care (Kakkad et al., 2014; Codjoe
et al., 2020). This distinction matters for interpretation: increased acute utilisation under heat
can reflect increased need (risk exposure) rather than improved access, while declines in routine
utilisation under floods can reflect barriers to both demand and supply.
Health system resilience theory provides a coherent lens for integrating these findings
and clarifying policy-relevant levers. Following Kruk et al. (2015), resilience is the capacity of
health actors, institutions, and populations to prepare for, respond to, and recover from shocks
while maintaining core functions. Blanchet et al. further conceptualise resilience as absorptive,
adaptive, and transformative capacity under stress (Blanchet et al., 2017). Within our evidence

51
base, many responses (mobile outreach, redeployment of staff, alternative transport, temporary
service relocation) primarily reflect absorptive and adaptive capacities (Ray-Bennett et al., 2021;
Purno et al., 2023; Saulnier et al., 2022; Wilunda et al., 2016; Quilty et al., 2024). Where floods
are repeated or severe and baseline infrastructure and governance are weak, these capacities
appear insufficient, resulting in sustained declines in service coverage and quality (Barman, Sarif
e Saha, 2023; Baten et al., 2020; Chandir et al., 2023).
Critically, resilience is not value-neutral. The resilience literature cautions that “coping”
can transfer costs to households and frontline workers and can obscure equity trade-offs if not
explicitly addressed (Witter et al., 2023). This critique aligns with our findings: disruptions
and adaptations are consistently conditioned by social vulnerability (unequal access to cooling,
differential mobility constraints, gendered decision-making), shaping who bears the burden
of shocks and who retains access to safe care (Cil e Kim, 2022; Kim, Lee e Rossin-Slater,
2021; Haque, Parr e Muhidin, 2019; Firoz et al., 2016). A realist, equity-centred resilience
framing therefore supports a dual focus: maintaining service availability and readiness (supply-
side resilience) while reducing household-level constraints and opportunity costs that shape
care-seeking under shock (demand-side resilience).
The heterogeneity in exposure measurement and study design reflects the fragmented
state of climate–health evidence. Flood exposure is quantified using diverse approaches (remote
sensing,administrativedatabases,self-reportedexposure),whileheatwavedefinitionsvarywidely
(absolute thresholds, percentiles, composite indices), limiting comparability across settings and
constraining meta-analytic synthesis. A coordinated methodological framework aligned with
established hazard definitions would strengthen cumulative knowledge production (Pörtner et al.,
2022). Moreover, the dominance of cross-sectional designs in flood studies and retrospective
acute-care analyses in heat studies limits inference on long-term, cumulative, and compounding
impacts, including repeated exposure and multi-hazard contexts.
These methodological patterns plausibly contribute to the observed evidence asymmetry:
heatresearchskewstowardacuteoutcomesinhospitaldatasetsfromhigh-incomecontexts,while
flood research concentrates in rural LMIC settings and focuses on routine service coverage.
This distribution narrows understanding of (i) heat impacts on routine maternal care and (ii)
flood impacts in urban contexts and underrepresented regions such as Latin America and the
Caribbean.
Our findings support a dual-track strategy to strengthen MCH resilience to climate
shocks. On the supply side, priorities include climate-resilient infrastructure (including thermal
safety and reliable power for cooling), strengthened logistics and supply chains, and workforce
protection and surge capacity to maintain service continuity during disruptions (Kakkad et al.,
2014; Codjoe et al., 2020). On the demand side, social protection mechanisms buffering income
loss and displacement, community-tailored preparedness plans, and trusted risk communication
are central to reducing delays in care-seeking and preventing harmful care avoidance or unsafe
care substitution (Ray-Bennett et al., 2021; Purno et al., 2023). Because utilisation under heat

52
may increase through heightened morbidity, planning should anticipate demand surges for acute
obstetric and neonatal care while explicitly protecting routine preventive services from being
crowded out.
Macro assessments highlight that climate hazards increasingly impose systemic burdens
and economic costs, reinforcing the value of proactive adaptation rather than reactive response
(Romanello et al., 2025; Pörtner et al., 2022). For MCH specifically, delays in routine care
generatedownstreamcoststhroughavoidablecomplications,whileacutesurgesstrainbudgetsand
capacity, both of which are central concerns in health economics and health system performance.
Future research should prioritise: (1) standardised hazard metrics (consistent thresholds
for heatwaves and flood severity) and transparent exposure operationalisation; (2) longitudinal
and mixed-methods designs that connect lived experiences to system-level outcomes and identify
causal mechanisms more credibly; (3) broader geographic coverage, including underrepresented
regions (Latin America and the Caribbean, for instance) and low-resource urban settings; (4)
explicit modelling of social vulnerability (income, gender, displacement, housing quality, access
to cooling) and care substitution dynamics (informal care, delayed care, service switching); and
(5)multi-hazardandcompounding-riskanalysesthatreflectreal-worldclimateriskprofilesrather
than single-event retrospection.
2.5 CONCLUSION
Overall, this realist-informed systematic review shows that floods and heatwaves disrupt
MCH service utilisation through distinct but overlapping pathways that are strongly conditioned
by baseline system capacity and social vulnerability. The evidence is most consistent for floods
suppressingroutineservices(ANC,facilitydelivery,PNC,immunisation)viamobilityconstraints,
displacement, income loss, and service disruption, whereas heat is more often linked to increases
in acute and emergency utilisation that reflect heightened maternal and neonatal risk and
operational stress. These findings imply that climate-resilient MCH strategies must protect both
access and facility functionality while reducing household-level barriers through preparedness
andsocialprotection.Majorgapsremain,includinglimitedevidenceonheat-relateddisruptionsto
routinecare,sparseresearchonchildservicesbeyondacuteuse,andunevengeographiccoverage,
underscoring the need for standardised exposure metrics and more longitudinal, mixed-methods,
and causal studies.

3 CAUSAL LOOP DIAGRAM
ABSTRACT
Background:Floods and heatwaves increasingly threaten maternal and child health
(MCH) by disrupting access to, and delivery of, essential services such as antenatal care, facility
delivery, postnatal care, and immunisation. However, the mechanisms through which these
hazards translate into changes in MCH utilisation remain insufficiently understood, limiting the
design of context-sensitive resilience policies.
Methods:Building on a realist-informed systematic review (Chapter 2), we developed a
Causal Loop Diagram (CLD) to synthesise heterogeneous evidence into an explanatory system
map. We extracted recurrent Context–Mechanism–Outcome (CMO) patterns, consolidated them
into six interacting mechanisms: (M1) impaired mobility, (M2) displacement, (M3) income loss,
(M4) increased health risks, (M5) service disruption, and (M6) energy/productivity/supply-chain
disruption. We translated these pathways into signed causal links and feedback structures.
Contextual variation was made explicit through classification of studies by rurality, national
income level, Köppen–Geiger climate zone, and health system type.
Results:The CLD identifies eighteen components distributed across the six mechanisms
and reveals multiple reinforcing feedback loops concentrated in livelihood and displacement
pathways. Flood impacts most consistently reduce routine MCH utilisation through concurrent
failuresintransport,livelihoods,facilityfunctionality,andsupplychains,particularlyinruraland
low-incomesettings.Heatevidenceismorecontext-specificandoftenreflectsashifttowardacute
utilisation (e.g., emergency care) and operational stress via energy dependence and workforce
strain. Across hazards, economic contraction and mobility constraints emerge as key upstream
drivers that can trigger cascading reductions in service use.
Conclusion:A realist-informed CLD provides a transparent, mechanism-based account
of how extreme weather events propagate through demand- and supply-side channels to shape
MCH utilisation. The model highlights leverage points beyond the health sector—particularly
income protection, transport continuity, and energy/logistics resilience—while underscoring
that causal strength and loop dominance remain uncertain without empirical validation. Future
work should validate the CLD with stakeholders and translate it into a stock-and-flow model to
quantify dynamics, delays, and policy impacts under single and compound hazards.
Keywords:Climate change. Floods. Heatwaves. Maternal and child health. Healthcare
utilisation. Realist synthesis. Systems thinking. Causal loop diagram. Health system resilience.

HIGHLIGHTS
• Develops a realist-informed Causal Loop Diagram to explain how floods and heatwaves
affect MCH utilisation.
• Identifies six interacting mechanisms spanning mobility, displacement, income, health
risks, service disruption, and infrastructure stress.
• Reveals reinforcing feedback loops concentrated in livelihood and displacement pathways
that can amplify utilisation losses.
• Shows hazard-specific signatures: floods predominantly suppress routine care; heat more
often induces operational stress and acute demand.
• Points to cross-sector leverage points (income protection, transport, energy and logistics
resilience) to strengthen MCH system resilience.
3.1 INTRODUCTION
Climatechangeisincreasingthefrequencyandintensityofextremeweatherevents,posing
significant risks to health systems by disrupting healthcare services, straining limited resources,
and exacerbating morbidity and mortality (Codjoe et al., 2020; Ebi et al., 2021; Chersich et al.,
2023). Floods and heatwaves are among the most frequent and devastating natural disasters,
disproportionately affecting low-income populations and threatening the continuity of essential
health services. Pregnant women and children are particularly vulnerable to this disruption.
Despite increasing recognition of these risks, there remains a persistent gap in understanding the
specific mechanisms through which floods and heatwaves disrupt maternal and child healthcare
(MCH)utilization.Thisgaplimitsthedevelopmentofeffective,context-sensitivepoliciescapable
of reducing adverse outcomes such as maternal and neonatal mortality, missed antenatal care,
and complications during childbirth (Meherali et al., 2024).
This study addresses that gap by integrating systems thinking into disaster-health analysis.
Our aim is to uncover how extreme weather events impact the delivery and use of MCH services,
by identifying key causal mechanisms and feedback structures that shape these disruptions and
proposing evidence-based strategies to improve MCH system resilience.
The central research question guiding this study is: Through which mechanisms do flood
and heatwaves impact access to and use of maternal and child health services?
MCH utilisation is the extent to which healthcare services designed to improve the health
outcomes of mothers and children - such as antenatal care, skilled birth attendance, postnatal
care, and immunizations - are accessed and used by the target population (Sarikhani, Najibi e
Razavi, 2024).
We hypothesize six main mechanisms that mediate this relationship:
•M1 - Impaired ability to travel.

97
•M2 - Displacement and migration of affected populations.
•M3 - Household income loss, reducing demand for services.
•M4 - Increased health risks and competing healthcare needs.
•M5 - Strain on healthcare supply and service availability.
•M6 - Disruption to energy, productivity and supply chain.
Thesemechanismsdonotoperateinisolation.Rather,theyinteractdynamically,sometimes
reinforcing one another through feedback loops, which may either exacerbate or mitigate the
effects of flooding on healthcare utilization. To explore these dynamics, we employ Causal Loop
Diagrams (CLDs), a qualitative systems thinking tools used to visually map causal relationships.
CLDsrepresentvariablesasnodesandusedirectionallinkstodenoteeitherreinforcing(positive)
or balancing (negative) interactions (Sterman, 2000; Strelkovskii e Rovenskaya, 2021).
For example, flood-induced road damage (M1) may reduce patients’ ability to reach
care, decreasing service utilization. This drop in demand may result in service contraction
(M5), strengthening the original access barrier and creating a self-reinforcing negative loop.
Alternatively, investment in mobile units or resilient infrastructure could create positive feedback
loops, helping restore or even improve service utilization. CLDs thus offer a structured lens to
examine system interactions and identify strategic points of intervention.
Our analytical framework draws inspiration from realist evaluation (Pawson e Tilley,
1997), which emphasizes context-mechanism-outcome (CMO) configurations. While not aiming
to test program effectiveness, this study seeks to refine the theoretical understanding of system
behaviour under environmental stress. By examining where demand- and supply-side disruptions
intersect, we aim to identify system vulnerabilities, leverage points, and potential tipping points.
The relevance of this study extends beyond public health, offering important contribu-
tions to the field of health economics. It sheds light on how climate-related shocks disrupt
service delivery, reduce productivity, and strain resource allocation. These disruptions generate
multidimensional economic costs (from lost labor days to increased healthcare expenditures)
with consequences for both local resilience and national policy planning. By identifying the
transmissionmechanismsthroughasystemsthinkinglens,thisstudyprovidesactionableinsights
for developing adaptive policies that mitigate long-term welfare losses. In doing so, it introduces
a novel CLD-based framework to the health economics literature, emphasizing the complex
economic pathways linking environmental shocks to maternal and child healthcare utilization.
Complex systems are sets of interconnected elements that interact dynamically and
nonlinearly, resulting in unpredictable, emergent behaviors that cannot be explained solely by
examining the isolated parts. Examples of such systems include ecosystems, financial markets, or
the human body. They are considered adaptive, meaning they can change and evolve in response
to the environment or internal interactions. Understanding these systems requires an approach

98
that considers the relationships among components and the patterns that emerge from these
interactions (Mitchell, 2009).
Health systems are increasingly viewed as complex adaptive systems (CAS), networks of
interdependent actors, institutions, and resources that evolve in response to shocks (Borghi et al.,
2022). These systems exhibit nonlinear dynamics, emergent behaviors, and feedback sensitivity,
which complicate efforts to manage them through linear policy responses (Mitchell, 2009; Khan
et al., 2018). As McNab et al. (2020) and Nason (2023) highlight, designing effective responses
to crises like floods requires recognizing and responding to the interconnectedness of social,
institutional, and environmental influences within the system.
System mapping, through tools like CLDs, offers a valuable approach to navigating
this complexity. It enables policymakers and practitioners to visualize dependencies, anticipate
unintended consequences, and align interventions across sectors. As Pype et al. (2018) note,
understandingtheperceptionsandinteractionsamonghealthsystemactorsenhancescoordination
and decision-making. When combined with evidence-based design principles (Engelseth et al.,
2021), system mapping strengthens strategic planning and supports more resilient and equitable
maternal and child healthcare in disaster-prone settings.
Based on this conceptual foundation, this study has three specific objectives: (i) to
identify and analyze the key mechanisms linking flood exposure to changes in maternal and child
healthcare utilization; (ii) to develop a Causal Loop Diagram that maps interactions, feedback
loops, and leverage points within the system; (iii) to propose evidence-informed strategies to
strengthen the resilience of MCH services in flood-prone contexts.
Beyond this Introduction (Section 3.1), the remainder of the essay is organized as follows.
Section 3.2 describes the methodological approach, detailing the rationale for using Causal Loop
Diagrams(CLDs).Section3.3presentsthefindings,includingthedevelopmentandinterpretation
of the causal model. Section 3.4 discusses the main results in light of the existing literature,
highlighting policy implications and avenues for future research. Finally, Section 3.5 concludes

3.2 METHODS
This section describes the methods used to develop an evidence-informed causal model
of how floods and heatwaves affect maternal and child healthcare utilisation. It first explains how
realist synthesis was used to identify and refine context–mechanism–outcome configurations
and then outlines how these findings were translated into a causal loop diagram to represent the
interactions, feedback structures, and pathways operating within the health system.
3.2.1 Realist synthesis
Realist synthesis (also referred to as realist review) is a theory-driven approach to
evidence synthesis rooted in scientific realism, designed to explain how and why outcomes

99
occur by uncovering the generative mechanisms that are triggered (or suppressed) in particular
contexts (Pawson e Tilley, 1997; Pawson, 2006). In contrast to conventional effectiveness-
focused reviews, realist synthesis asks: what works, for whom, in what circumstances, and
through what mechanisms? It conceptualises causality through Context–Mechanism–Outcome
(CMO) configurations, where outcomes arise from the interaction between contextual conditions
(e.g., geography, institutions, socioeconomic vulnerability) and mechanisms (e.g., behavioural
responses, resource constraints, organisational adaptation).
This approach is particularly appropriate for analysing extreme weather events (EWEs)
and maternal and child health (MCH) utilisation because floods and heatwaves function as
complex exogenous shocks, not discrete interventions. They perturb multiple system domains
simultaneously (mobility and access, household livelihoods, disease risks, facility functionality,
workforce capacity, and supply chains) often producing nonlinear effects and feedback (e.g.,
temporary access barriers translating into longer-term service contraction or risk escalation).
Recent syntheses of EWEs and healthcare utilisation in rural/remote contexts highlight precisely
this multi-pathway disruption and the importance of examining mechanisms and context-
dependence rather than relying solely on average effects (Dewi et al., 2024). Given that health
systems are increasingly analysed as complex adaptive systems (Borghi et al., 2022), realist
synthesis is well suited to explaining why the same hazard can generate different utilisation
outcomes across places and populations, depending on pre-existing vulnerability, institutional
buffering, and adaptive capacity.
Inthisthesis,therealist-informedsynthesis(Chapter2)providedtheevidentiaryfoundation
for the CLD by (i) extracting and refining mechanism-based explanations from heterogeneous
study designs and (ii) translating recurrent CMO patterns into a coherent causal architecture. The
review followed structured searching and screening procedures consistent with contemporary
systematic-review reporting norms (PRISMA 2020), while preserving the realist principle
of iterative theory refinement (i.e., searching and interpretation continued until the emerging
programme theory adequately explained observed patterns) (Akl et al., 2024). Evidence was
not ranked using a traditional hierarchy. Instead, documents were appraised for their relevance
(capacity to inform theory building/testing), richness (depth of causal explanation), and rigour
(credibility of the methods generating the specific data used for theory refinement), in line with
updated realist methodological guidance (Dada et al., 2023).
Data extraction was organised to identify and compare (a) Contexts (C): structural and
situational features shaping vulnerability and response (e.g., rurality and remoteness, baseline
infrastructure,facilitydensity,governancecoordination,povertyandinformality,socialprotection
coverage, existing service quality) (Greenhalgh e Manzano, 2022; Renmans, Holvoet e Criel,
2020); (b) Mechanisms (M): underlying processes activated by the hazard (e.g., reduced ability
to travel; displacement; income loss and reallocation of time; heightened clinical risk and com-
peting care needs; reduced service availability through facility damage/overcrowding/workforce
depletion; energy and supply-chain disruption) (Shaw et al., 2018; Dalkin et al., 2015); and (c)

100
Outcomes (O): observable changes in MCH utilisation (e.g., missed or delayed antenatal care,
reduced facility delivery or skilled attendance, disruptions to postnatal care and immunisation,
shifts from routine to emergency care) (Sarikhani, Najibi e Razavi, 2024; Shanto et al., 2023;
Tiruneh et al., 2022). This structure also aligned with established access/utilisation conceptu-
alisations that separate demand-side constraints from supply-side capacity, while recognising
their interaction (e.g., perceived need, affordability, acceptability, and availability) (Andersen,
2008).ThesynthesisiterativelycomparedCMOsacrosssettingstoidentifyrecurringexplanatory
patterns and to consolidate them into higher-order mechanisms that were sufficiently general to
travel across contexts, but specific enough to support causal mapping.

and availability; and (M6) disruption of energy, productivity, and supply chains. Importantly,
the realist synthesis emphasised that these pathways are seldom independent: they co-occur and
may generate reinforcing dynamics (e.g., facility disruption lowers service quality and trust,
which further reduces utilisation even after physical access is restored) or balancing dynamics
(e.g., emergency mobilisation temporarily expands outreach capacity). This is precisely where
realist synthesis becomes methodologically complementary to systems thinking: realist synthesis
specifies what mechanisms are plausible and evidenced, while system mapping formalises how
those mechanisms interact over time and through feedback.
Accordingly,thefinalstageoftherealistsynthesisconsistedoftranslationfromprogramme
theory to system structure. Mechanisms and their associated variables were converted into CLD
nodes and signed causal links based on the directionality supported by the evidence. This
integration is consistent with recent methodological work that explicitly combines realist theory-
building with causal loop diagramming as an approach to unpack complexity in health systems
research, including in LMIC settings (Cassidy et al., 2022; Ehteshami et al., 2024). The CLD
thereby functions as a structured representation of the realist programme theory: CMOs become
connected causal chains; recurring CMOs form feedback loops; and leverage points emerge
where interventions may interrupt reinforcing cycles of disruption or strengthen stabilising
responses. The end result is an evidence-informed explanatory model of how climate-related
