3.1 INTRODUCTION
Climatechangeisincreasingthefrequencyandintensityofextremeweatherevents,posing
significant risks to health systems by disrupting healthcare services, straining limited resources,
and exacerbating morbidity and mortality (Codjoe et al., 2020; Ebi et al., 2021; Chersich et al.,
2023). Floods and heatwaves are among the most frequent and devastating natural disasters,
disproportionately affecting low-income populations and threatening the continuity of essential
health services. Pregnant women and children are particularly vulnerable to this disruption.
Despite increasing recognition of these risks, there remains a persistent gap in understanding the
specific mechanisms through which floods and heatwaves disrupt maternal and child healthcare
(MCH)utilization.Thisgaplimitsthedevelopmentofeffective,context-sensitivepoliciescapable
of reducing adverse outcomes such as maternal and neonatal mortality, missed antenatal care,
and complications during childbirth (Meherali et al., 2024).
This study addresses that gap by integrating systems thinking into disaster-health analysis.
Our aim is to uncover how extreme weather events impact the delivery and use of MCH services,
by identifying key causal mechanisms and feedback structures that shape these disruptions and
proposing evidence-based strategies to improve MCH system resilience.
The central research question guiding this study is: Through which mechanisms do flood
and heatwaves impact access to and use of maternal and child health services?
MCH utilisation is the extent to which healthcare services designed to improve the health
outcomes of mothers and children - such as antenatal care, skilled birth attendance, postnatal
care, and immunizations - are accessed and used by the target population (Sarikhani, Najibi e
Razavi, 2024).
We hypothesize six main mechanisms that mediate this relationship:
•M1 - Impaired ability to travel.

97
•M2 - Displacement and migration of affected populations.
•M3 - Household income loss, reducing demand for services.
•M4 - Increased health risks and competing healthcare needs.
•M5 - Strain on healthcare supply and service availability.
•M6 - Disruption to energy, productivity and supply chain.
Thesemechanismsdonotoperateinisolation.Rather,theyinteractdynamically,sometimes
reinforcing one another through feedback loops, which may either exacerbate or mitigate the
effects of flooding on healthcare utilization. To explore these dynamics, we employ Causal Loop
Diagrams (CLDs), a qualitative systems thinking tools used to visually map causal relationships.
CLDsrepresentvariablesasnodesandusedirectionallinkstodenoteeitherreinforcing(positive)
or balancing (negative) interactions (Sterman, 2000; Strelkovskii e Rovenskaya, 2021).
For example, flood-induced road damage (M1) may reduce patients’ ability to reach
care, decreasing service utilization. This drop in demand may result in service contraction
(M5), strengthening the original access barrier and creating a self-reinforcing negative loop.
Alternatively, investment in mobile units or resilient infrastructure could create positive feedback
loops, helping restore or even improve service utilization. CLDs thus offer a structured lens to
examine system interactions and identify strategic points of intervention.
Our analytical framework draws inspiration from realist evaluation (Pawson e Tilley,
1997), which emphasizes context-mechanism-outcome (CMO) configurations. While not aiming
to test program effectiveness, this study seeks to refine the theoretical understanding of system
behaviour under environmental stress. By examining where demand- and supply-side disruptions
intersect, we aim to identify system vulnerabilities, leverage points, and potential tipping points.
The relevance of this study extends beyond public health, offering important contribu-
tions to the field of health economics. It sheds light on how climate-related shocks disrupt
service delivery, reduce productivity, and strain resource allocation. These disruptions generate
multidimensional economic costs (from lost labor days to increased healthcare expenditures)
with consequences for both local resilience and national policy planning. By identifying the
transmissionmechanismsthroughasystemsthinkinglens,thisstudyprovidesactionableinsights
for developing adaptive policies that mitigate long-term welfare losses. In doing so, it introduces
a novel CLD-based framework to the health economics literature, emphasizing the complex
economic pathways linking environmental shocks to maternal and child healthcare utilization.
Complex systems are sets of interconnected elements that interact dynamically and
nonlinearly, resulting in unpredictable, emergent behaviors that cannot be explained solely by
examining the isolated parts. Examples of such systems include ecosystems, financial markets, or
the human body. They are considered adaptive, meaning they can change and evolve in response
to the environment or internal interactions. Understanding these systems requires an approach

98
that considers the relationships among components and the patterns that emerge from these
interactions (Mitchell, 2009).
Health systems are increasingly viewed as complex adaptive systems (CAS), networks of
interdependent actors, institutions, and resources that evolve in response to shocks (Borghi et al.,
2022). These systems exhibit nonlinear dynamics, emergent behaviors, and feedback sensitivity,
which complicate efforts to manage them through linear policy responses (Mitchell, 2009; Khan
et al., 2018). As McNab et al. (2020) and Nason (2023) highlight, designing effective responses
to crises like floods requires recognizing and responding to the interconnectedness of social,
institutional, and environmental influences within the system.
System mapping, through tools like CLDs, offers a valuable approach to navigating
this complexity. It enables policymakers and practitioners to visualize dependencies, anticipate
unintended consequences, and align interventions across sectors. As Pype et al. (2018) note,
understandingtheperceptionsandinteractionsamonghealthsystemactorsenhancescoordination
and decision-making. When combined with evidence-based design principles (Engelseth et al.,
2021), system mapping strengthens strategic planning and supports more resilient and equitable
maternal and child healthcare in disaster-prone settings.
Based on this conceptual foundation, this study has three specific objectives: (i) to
identify and analyze the key mechanisms linking flood exposure to changes in maternal and child
healthcare utilization; (ii) to develop a Causal Loop Diagram that maps interactions, feedback
loops, and leverage points within the system; (iii) to propose evidence-informed strategies to
strengthen the resilience of MCH services in flood-prone contexts.
Beyond this Introduction (Section 3.1), the remainder of the essay is organized as follows.
Section 3.2 describes the methodological approach, detailing the rationale for using Causal Loop
Diagrams(CLDs).Section3.3presentsthefindings,includingthedevelopmentandinterpretation
of the causal model. Section 3.4 discusses the main results in light of the existing literature,
highlighting policy implications and avenues for future research. Finally, Section 3.5 concludes
the essay.
3.2 METHODS
This section describes the methods used to develop an evidence-informed causal model
of how floods and heatwaves affect maternal and child healthcare utilisation. It first explains how
realist synthesis was used to identify and refine context–mechanism–outcome configurations
and then outlines how these findings were translated into a causal loop diagram to represent the
interactions, feedback structures, and pathways operating within the health system.
3.2.1 Realist synthesis
Realist synthesis (also referred to as realist review) is a theory-driven approach to
evidence synthesis rooted in scientific realism, designed to explain how and why outcomes

99
occur by uncovering the generative mechanisms that are triggered (or suppressed) in particular
contexts (Pawson e Tilley, 1997; Pawson, 2006). In contrast to conventional effectiveness-
focused reviews, realist synthesis asks: what works, for whom, in what circumstances, and
through what mechanisms? It conceptualises causality through Context–Mechanism–Outcome
(CMO) configurations, where outcomes arise from the interaction between contextual conditions
(e.g., geography, institutions, socioeconomic vulnerability) and mechanisms (e.g., behavioural
responses, resource constraints, organisational adaptation).
This approach is particularly appropriate for analysing extreme weather events (EWEs)
and maternal and child health (MCH) utilisation because floods and heatwaves function as
complex exogenous shocks, not discrete interventions. They perturb multiple system domains
simultaneously (mobility and access, household livelihoods, disease risks, facility functionality,
workforce capacity, and supply chains) often producing nonlinear effects and feedback (e.g.,
temporary access barriers translating into longer-term service contraction or risk escalation).
Recent syntheses of EWEs and healthcare utilisation in rural/remote contexts highlight precisely
this multi-pathway disruption and the importance of examining mechanisms and context-
dependence rather than relying solely on average effects (Dewi et al., 2024). Given that health
systems are increasingly analysed as complex adaptive systems (Borghi et al., 2022), realist
synthesis is well suited to explaining why the same hazard can generate different utilisation
outcomes across places and populations, depending on pre-existing vulnerability, institutional
buffering, and adaptive capacity.
Inthisthesis,therealist-informedsynthesis(Chapter2)providedtheevidentiaryfoundation
for the CLD by (i) extracting and refining mechanism-based explanations from heterogeneous
study designs and (ii) translating recurrent CMO patterns into a coherent causal architecture. The
review followed structured searching and screening procedures consistent with contemporary
systematic-review reporting norms (PRISMA 2020), while preserving the realist principle
of iterative theory refinement (i.e., searching and interpretation continued until the emerging
programme theory adequately explained observed patterns) (Akl et al., 2024). Evidence was
not ranked using a traditional hierarchy. Instead, documents were appraised for their relevance
(capacity to inform theory building/testing), richness (depth of causal explanation), and rigour
(credibility of the methods generating the specific data used for theory refinement), in line with
updated realist methodological guidance (Dada et al., 2023).
Data extraction was organised to identify and compare (a) Contexts (C): structural and
situational features shaping vulnerability and response (e.g., rurality and remoteness, baseline
infrastructure,facilitydensity,governancecoordination,povertyandinformality,socialprotection
coverage, existing service quality) (Greenhalgh e Manzano, 2022; Renmans, Holvoet e Criel,
2020); (b) Mechanisms (M): underlying processes activated by the hazard (e.g., reduced ability
to travel; displacement; income loss and reallocation of time; heightened clinical risk and com-
peting care needs; reduced service availability through facility damage/overcrowding/workforce
depletion; energy and supply-chain disruption) (Shaw et al., 2018; Dalkin et al., 2015); and (c)

100
Outcomes (O): observable changes in MCH utilisation (e.g., missed or delayed antenatal care,
reduced facility delivery or skilled attendance, disruptions to postnatal care and immunisation,
shifts from routine to emergency care) (Sarikhani, Najibi e Razavi, 2024; Shanto et al., 2023;
Tiruneh et al., 2022). This structure also aligned with established access/utilisation conceptu-
alisations that separate demand-side constraints from supply-side capacity, while recognising
their interaction (e.g., perceived need, affordability, acceptability, and availability) (Andersen,
2008).ThesynthesisiterativelycomparedCMOsacrosssettingstoidentifyrecurringexplanatory
patterns and to consolidate them into higher-order mechanisms that were sufficiently general to
travel across contexts, but specific enough to support causal mapping.
Theresultingprogrammetheory,groundedinthereviewedevidence,wassummarisedinto
sixinteractingpathwayslinkingfloodsandheatwavestoMCHutilisation:(M1)impairedmobility
andphysicalaccess;(M2)displacementandmigration;(M3)incomelossandeconomicinsecurity;
(M4)increasedhealthrisksandcompetinghealthcareneeds;(M5)strainonhealth-servicesupply
and availability; and (M6) disruption of energy, productivity, and supply chains. Importantly,
the realist synthesis emphasised that these pathways are seldom independent: they co-occur and
may generate reinforcing dynamics (e.g., facility disruption lowers service quality and trust,
which further reduces utilisation even after physical access is restored) or balancing dynamics
(e.g., emergency mobilisation temporarily expands outreach capacity). This is precisely where
realist synthesis becomes methodologically complementary to systems thinking: realist synthesis
specifies what mechanisms are plausible and evidenced, while system mapping formalises how
those mechanisms interact over time and through feedback.
Accordingly,thefinalstageoftherealistsynthesisconsistedoftranslationfromprogramme
theory to system structure. Mechanisms and their associated variables were converted into CLD
nodes and signed causal links based on the directionality supported by the evidence. This
integration is consistent with recent methodological work that explicitly combines realist theory-
building with causal loop diagramming as an approach to unpack complexity in health systems
research, including in LMIC settings (Cassidy et al., 2022; Ehteshami et al., 2024). The CLD
thereby functions as a structured representation of the realist programme theory: CMOs become
connected causal chains; recurring CMOs form feedback loops; and leverage points emerge
where interventions may interrupt reinforcing cycles of disruption or strengthen stabilising
responses. The end result is an evidence-informed explanatory model of how climate-related
hazardspropagatethroughdemand-andsupply-sidechannelstoshapeMCHutilisation,providing
atransparentbasisforidentifyingresiliencestrategiesthataresensitivetocontextandmechanism
rather than “one-size-fits-all” prescriptions.
3.2.2 Causal loop diagrams
Causalloopdiagrams(CLDs)areafoundationaltoolinsystemsthinkingusedtorepresent
and analyze the dynamic cause-and-effect relationships within complex systems. Originating
in the system dynamics tradition (Forrester, 2012), CLDs enable researchers to visualize how

101
variablesinteract,influenceoneanotherovertime,andgeneratefeedbackloops(eitherreinforcing
or balancing) that shape system behavior (Sterman, 2000).
In CLDs, variables are connected by arrows that indicate the direction and nature of
influence:positivelinksdenotechangesinthesamedirection,whilenegativelinksimplyopposing
effects (Strelkovskii e Rovenskaya, 2021). These diagrams are particularly useful for identifying
feedback structures and leverage points in systems where interventions often produce non-linear
and unintended consequences.
Since the 1970s, CLDs have been applied in public health to model complex problems
such as drug addiction (Levin, Roberts e Hirsch, 1975), infectious disease dynamics (Ritchie-
DunhameGalván,1999),andhealthcarepolicydesign(Roystonetal.,1999).Theseearlystudies
demonstrated how feedback mechanisms explain persistent challenges in health systems and
highlighted the importance of visualizing systemic interdependencies for policy planning.
From the mid-2000s onward, public health scholars increasingly advocated for systems
thinking, and CLDs gained traction as tools to improve health systems analysis (Homer e Hirsch,
2006;LeischoweMilstein,2006;SavignyeAdam,2009).Morerecently,CLDshavebeenwidely
appliedtoexplorematernalandchildhealthissuesacrossdiversecontexts.Forinstance,Zafaretal.
(2023) mapped disruptions to MCH services during the COVID-19 pandemic in Pakistan, while
Cassidy et al. (2021) examined how pay-for-performance schemes influenced MCH coverage
in Tanzania. In Malawi, Hamon et al. (2022) used CLDs to analyze the integration of family
planning with child immunization services. Lemke et al. (2023) collaborated with communities
in Texas to investigate how structural racism contributes to maternal morbidity among Black
women. Similarly, Brereton e Jagals (2021) explored the complex causal relationships linking
poverty, environmental factors, and child health outcomes in low- and middle-income countries.
Recent studies have increasingly integrated realist evaluation and systematic reviews with
Causal Loop Diagrams (CLDs) to better understand how contextual factors and mechanisms
interact to produce outcomes in complex health systems. For example, Ehteshami et al. (2024)
combined realist logic with CLDs to model care pathways for diabetes and hypertension in
low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), while Mukumbang et al. (2022) employed critical
realist synthesis to uncover generative mechanisms in community-based care. Poix e Elmusharaf
(2023) used meta-analyses to construct CLDs linking preconception care to maternal and child
health outcomes. Similarly, Renmans, Holvoet e Criel (2020) and Singh et al. (2021) applied
realist-informed CLDs to analyze performance-based financing schemes, demonstrating how
interventions operate differently across settings depending on local context.
InBrazil,CausalLoopDiagrams(CLDs)havebeenincreasinglyusedtoexaminecomplex
dynamics within the Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS). Carpes (2024) developed a CLD based on
interviews and process data to investigate failures in surgical scheduling, highlighting how issues
related to communication, training, and technology contribute to poor data quality, which in turn
reinforces ineffective decision-making. Similarly, Bergiante et al. (2024) mapped national-level
causal links in the organ transplant system, revealing systemic inefficiencies. By combining CLD

102
analysis with Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA), their study identified mismatches between
resources and outcomes across states, demonstrating the value of integrating qualitative systems
mapping with quantitative performance evaluation to uncover feedback-driven bottlenecks in
health service delivery.
According to Mueller (2015), the use of complex adaptive systems modelling techniques
in the public policy cycle in Brazil remains incipient, despite growing academic interest in the
topic. He argues that this gap reflects, in part, the relatively early diffusion of complexity ideas
and, above all, the tension between the dominant policy-making logic (characterised by central
planning, target-setting, control, and a strong reliance on information) and the nature of complex
systems, in which heterogeneous agents interact locally under bounded rationality, producing
emergent outcomes that are difficult to anticipate and control. In this context, Mueller (2015)
contends that complex systems modelling can help reorient Brazilian public policies by shifting
the focus from the “precise control” of outcomes toward the capacity to influence systemic
properties (e.g., interdependence, connectivity, diversity, and adaptability). This is particularly
relevantforpublichealthandforBrazil’sUnifiedHealthSystem(SUS),aprototypicallycomplex
domain with multiple levels of governance, service networks, budget constraints, and adaptive
responsesbyprofessionalsandusers,wherelinearinterventionsandsinglemetricsoftengenerate
unexpected effects and, at times, perverse incentives (Mueller, 2015).
The CLD presented in this study was developed based on the evidence synthesized in the
Realist-Informed Systematic Review (Chapter 2), which assessed the impacts of flood events on
maternal and child healthcare utilization. That review provided a comprehensive understanding
of how floods affect both the demand for and supply of health services, shaping MCH outcomes
through complex, interacting mechanisms.
Drawingfromtheliterature,weidentifiedkeyvariablesandcausalprocessesthatinfluence
maternal and child healthcare (MCH) during extreme weather events. These processes, which we
refer to as mechanisms or pathways, represent the chains of cause and effect linking exposure to
floods and heatwaves with changes in MCH utilization. These insights informed the structure
of our Causal Loop Diagram (CLD), allowing us to map dynamic interactions, feedback loops,
and potential policy leverage points. The CLD was developed using Kumu (2026), a free,
web-based platform for building interactive systems maps. It visually represents the components
and connections that shape how floods affect healthcare access and delivery.
3.3 RESULTS
Based on the previously conducted systematic literature review (Chapter 2), we identified
eighteen components distributed in six main mechanisms that link exposure to floods and
heatwaves to outcomes related to the utilization of maternal and child health (MCH) services.
Thesemechanismsprovideadetailedviewofthedynamicsthatwillbepresentedinthecomplete
CLD: (M1) restriction to travel, (M2) displacement and migration, (M3) income loss, (M4)
increased health risks, (M5) health service disruption and (M6) general infrastructure damage.

103
Furthermore, we highlight the interactions among these mechanisms, which play a crucial
role in understanding the overall system dynamics. Every component definition is presented in
Appendix 3.A.
Table 3.1 synthesises the empirical literature by aligning each study’s extreme weather
event and observed service outcomes with the mechanisms (M1–M6) identified in this thesis,
while explicitly locating those CMO patterns within a structured context framework. This table
therefore operationalises the realist logic of “what happens, through which mechanisms, and
under what contextual conditions”, and provides the bridge from evidence synthesis to system
mapping (realist programme theory to CLD structure), consistent with realist reporting standards
and mechanism-oriented synthesis (Wong et al., 2013; Page et al., 2021).
A central implication of realist synthesis is that the same shock (e.g., flooding) can
generate different utilisation outcomes because contexts condition whether and how mechanisms
fire. For climate-related shocks, this is especially important: hazards interact with settlement
patterns, economic vulnerability, climatic baselines, and institutional arrangements in ways that
shape both demand-side and supply-side disruption, including infrastructure failures, workforce
strain, and supply-chain interruptions (World Health Organization, 2022; Hartinger et al., 2025).
To make these contextual contingencies analytically transparent (and comparable across
studies), we classify each study along four dimensions:
a) Population context (Rural/Urban):Rurality is a first-order determinant of physical
access because it proxies longer travel times, greater reliance on vulnerable transport
routes, and thinner service networks (Dewi et al., 2024; Valente et al., 2026). In Table 3.1,
rural and remote settings are where mobility constraints (M1) and displacement (M2)
most consistently translate into declines in routine MCH utilisation (ANC, PNC, facility
delivery). This aligns with broader evidence that extreme events disproportionately impair
healthcare utilisation and outcomes in rural/remote populations via transport fragility and
service scarcity.
b) Economic context (High/Middle/Low income):Income level is a compact indicator of
baseline resilience: household buffers (savings, insurance coverage, social protection),
infrastructure quality, and surge capacity. Lower-income contexts tend to amplify income
shocks (M3) and supply strain (M5), increasing the probability that disruptions propagate
from short-term barriers to prolonged service interruption. Climate–health assessments
emphasise that vulnerability and impacts are uneven and strongly conditioned by devel-
opment and institutional capacity (Dagneau, Ehgartner e Gulis, 2025; Hartinger et al.,
2025).
c) Climate (Köppen–Geiger classification):Using the Köppen–Geiger system allows us
to place each extreme weather event within a comparable climatic regime defined by
long-term temperature and precipitation patterns. This matters because impacts depend on
what populations and health systems are accustomed to. Seasonality shapes adaptation:

104
historically hot regions are more likely to have cooling infrastructure and preparedness
for heat stress, whereas colder regions may be more vulnerable as temperatures rise and
heatwaves become more frequent. Likewise, changing precipitation patterns can make
previously low-risk areas flood-prone, where infrastructure and emergency systems were
not designed for such events. Classifying studies by Köppen zones therefore captures both
baseline climate conditions and the degree of preparedness embedded in local systems,
helpingexplainwhysimilarhazardstriggerdifferentmechanismsandvulnerabilitiesacross
settings (Günsche et al., 2026; Lima et al., 2023).
d) Health system (Universal/Mixed/Private):Health system type conditions both who
can access care under stress and how services adapt. Mixed systems (where government
services operate alongside private markets) are common in LMICs and are explicitly
discussed in the mixed-systems literature; they may create fragmented surge response,
uneven financial protection, and heterogeneous service availability across providers.
Conversely, universal/publicly administered arrangements may offer stronger baseline
financial protection and coordinated response capacity, while market-oriented systems can
exhibit utilisation shifts that are more visible in emergency settings and administrative
datasets.Comparativeworkonsystemtypologiesandpublic–privateconfigurationsupports
the analytical value of classifying systems along this axis when interpreting access and
utilisation patterns (Reibling, Ariaans e Wendt, 2019; Molander, 2025).
These four dimensions define the context space within which CMOs are interpreted.
They also guide the CLD: the same mechanism (e.g., M1 travel impairment) can yield different
feedbackdynamicsdependingonrurality,poverty,climateregime,andsystemfinancing/provision
structure.

3.3.1 Restrictions to travel (M1)
Mechanism 1, illustrated in Figure 3.1, links floods and heatwaves to MCH service
utilisationbydamagingtransportationinfrastructure,constrainingphysicalmobility,andreducing
willingness to travel under extreme conditions. Together, these factors shape whether, when,
and what type of care women and children can access. Travel restrictions affect MCH services
asymmetrically,loweringroutineserviceusewhileincreasingthelikelihoodthatcare(ifaccessed
at all) occurs late and through emergency pathways.
Figure 3.1 – Restriction to Travel Mechanism (M1)
Source: Prepared by the author.
3.3.1.1 Floods
Floods frequently damage roads and bridges, and disrupt transportation systems, cutting
off access to healthcare services by preventing ambulances or other vehicles from traveling
(Wilunda et al., 2016). These challenges are particularly acute for pregnant women. In obstetric
emergencies, when vehicles cannot reach communities due to flooding, women often rely on
improvisedtransport,suchasbeingcarriedbyfamilymembers(Wilundaetal.,2016).Inseasonal
flooding during the rainy season in Rumbek North County, South Sudan, water levels can rise
to shoulder height, making it physically impossible for pregnant women to walk or swim to
safety and rendering access to health facilities infeasible due to submerged terrain, washed-away
roads, and unsafe travel conditions (Wilunda et al., 2017). Whereas urban regions may offer
multiple routes and have more health facilities, rural populations are left with limited alternatives
and therefore face heightened risks of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality due to
geographic isolation (Mroz et al., 2023).
For example, in rural southern Mozambique, seasonal flooding transforms already
deteriorated roads into impassable terrain, leaving women with few transport options and
often forcing long, difficult journeys on foot or reliance on costly emergency travel. In these
settings, community members frequently step in to offer accompaniment or lend vehicles, which
underscores the critical role of social support (Firoz et al., 2016). Modelling work further shows

111
thatfloods candrasticallyextendtraveltimesand,in somecases,completelyisolatecommunities
for weeks or even months, denying pregnant women both routine and emergency care when it is
neededmost(Makangaetal.,2017).Similarly,duringthemajor2010Pakistanfloods,widespread
roaddamageandinundatedclinicsseverelydisruptedserviceavailabilityandimposedlongtravel
distances (often more than five kilometres), while limited financial resources prevented families
from accessing private care, leaving pregnant women and young children dependent on strained
public facilities that were themselves difficult to reach (Sadia et al., 2016).
Economic conditions critically shape whether families can overcome flood-related
transport barriers to reach care. In Bangladesh, for example, emergency boat travel may be
available during floods, but it is often prohibitively expensive as boatmen demand a high amount
ofmoneyfortheemergencyboattransportation(Abdullahetal.,2019).Hencepoorerhouseholds
are especially vulnerable to these constraints. Submerged roads and damaged transport networks
can force clinics to reduce hours or relocate, deplete essential supplies, increase referrals, and
ultimately leave many pregnant women and young children unable to complete those referrals
because alternative transport options are too costly, creating major financial barriers to accessing
essential maternal and child healthcare (Shah, Miller e Mothabbir, 2019).
3.3.1.2 Heatwaves
Bishwakarma(2022)suggeststhatinruralNepal,wherewomenoftenwalklongdistances
or rely on limited transport, high temperatures may discourage ANC attendance by increasing
physical discomfort during travel. However, the evidence remains tentative. The study finds an
inverse association between high-temperature days during gestation and total ANC visits but
cannot determine whether heat causes a sustained reduction in care or merely postpones visits to
cooler periods. Because it relies on aggregate counts without examining timing or substitution,
the persistence, clinical relevance, and underlying mechanism of the observed effect remain
unclear.
Quilty et al. (2024) examine the association between high temperatures and aeromedical
retrievals in the Northern Territory of Australia, a highly specific setting characterised by vast
distances, limited local clinical capacity, and reliance on air transport for emergency care. The
study finds a dose-response increase in obstetric retrievals during hotter periods in the humid
zone and in surgical retrievals in the arid zone, pointing to heightened heat-related morbidity
rather than direct disruption of care. Although retrieval services are reported to operate at or
near capacity year-round, the evidence does not demonstrate observed service overload, delays,
or unmet need; moreover, because heat exposure is operationalised using a 3-day lagged mean
temperature and local quartiles, the analysis does not distinguish discrete heatwave events from
broader seasonal heat. The authors therefore infer that increased demand for high-urgency
obstetric retrievals may constrain capacity for other cases, indicating a potential system-level
vulnerability in emergency transport logistics under extreme heat, rather than demonstrating
observed delays or denial of care.

112
3.3.2 Population displacement (M2)
To date, Mechanism 2 is unique to floods. As illustrated in Figure 3.2, it links flooding
to MCH service utilisation through displacement, understood as forced evacuation, temporary
sheltering, or longer-term migration following the destruction of homes, land, and livelihoods.
Displacement affects MCH service use by disrupting continuity of care, straining health system
functioning, and altering women and children’s ability and willingness to seek services. In this
way, Mechanism 2 captures the direct impacts of flooding on households and property and their
downstream consequences for MCH service utilisation.
Figure 3.2 – Population Displacement Mechanism (M2)
Source: Prepared by the author.
Floods can result in widespread destruction of properties and homes, leaving people
homeless and without livelihoods. Loss of or damage to housing forces evacuations (Jacquet
et al., 2016). After the 2022 Bangladesh floods, many community members took shelter inside
health facilities, which further disrupted service delivery and contributed to temporary loss of
routine SRHR and emergency perinatal services (Purno et al., 2023).
In flood prone regions, the increased frequency and intensity of floods, along with
riverbank erosion, led to the complete destruction of land and homes, making it impossible for
many families to return to their homes (Haque, Parr e Muhidin, 2019). This phenomenon is
linked to migration, driven by factors such as food insecurity, social marginalization, and lack of
access to institutional services, including healthcare and transportation (Haque, Parr e Muhidin,
2020b).
Migration resulting from displacement has a direct impact on the utilisation of MCH
services.Migrantwomen,especiallythosemovingfromruraltourbanareasorlivinginprecarious
settlements, face significant barriers to accessing antenatal care. These include a perceived low
need for care, lower sociocultural status, reduced social networks, lack of awareness of available
health services, and socioeconomic instability (Haque, Parr e Muhidin, 2020a). Moreover, newly
migrated women tend to use healthcare services less frequently than local resident populations,
with lower rates of antenatal visits among rural migrants (Haque, Parr e Muhidin, 2020a).
Infrastructuredamagefurtherintensifiesdisplacementpressures.Floodscandestroyroads,
bridges, and communication networks, halting economic activity and prolonging disruption long
after waters recede, often forcing households to relocate in search of basic services (Amoo et
al., 2018). Economic resources also shape mobility options: wealthier families can sometimes
evacuate early or employ protective strategies, whereas poorer households are more likely to be
permanently displaced without adequate access to care (Barman, Sarif e Saha, 2023). Affluent

113
populationsoftenavoidflood-proneareas,whereasmorevulnerablecommunitiesremaininthese
high-risk regions, increasing their exposure to disasters and their consequences (Orderud et al.,
2022).
Disaster preparedness directly affects whether pregnant women and children can travel to
safety in an emergency. In flood-prone areas with no prior evacuation plans, roads can become
impassableorunsafe,preventingtimelyrelocationbeforeorduringaflood(Surekha,Anbazhagan
e Kiran, 2020). Baten et al. (2020) emphasize early evacuation for pregnant women to minimize
exposure to severe events, a strategy that inherently depends on having reliable transportation
routes and methods. However, as Sadia et al. (2016) note, women are often excluded from
practical drills and skill-building activities, such as swimming lessons or training on navigating
collapsed structures.
3.3.3 Household income loss (M3)
Mechanism 3, shown in Figure 3.3, captures how floods and heatwaves affect agriculture,
livestock, businesses, and property, thereby reducing household income and limiting families’
capacity to access MCH services. Income loss influences MCH utilisation by lowering the ability
to pay for care, shifting household spending away from preventive services, and encouraging
delays or substitution with lower-cost alternatives, resulting in fewer routine contacts and greater
reliance on late, informal, or emergency care, effects that are most clearly documented for floods
and suggested more indirectly for heat.
Figure 3.3 – Income Loss Mechanism (M3)
Source: Prepared by the author.
3.3.3.1 Floods
Floods often devastate crops and livestock in farming communities, leaving rural popu-
lations who rely on the land for their livelihoods in extreme vulnerability and in greater need
of humanitarian assistance (Jacquet et al., 2016). This economic impact is aggravated by the

114
collapseofessentialinfrastructure,suchasroadsandbridges,andbytheshutdownofagricultural
and industrial activities; resulting in a significant loss of jobs and income as noted in studies
where up to 70% of people lost their means of subsistence after floods (Amoo et al., 2018).
The reduction in post-flood income directly affects families’ financial capacity to access
health services. In many cases, the cost of medical care is identified as the main barrier to
obtaining required services. For example, over half of flood-affected families reported having
to pay for health services even when their monthly income post-disaster was extremely low,
rendering those costs unfeasible within many families’ economic context (Jacquet et al., 2016).
In the case of pregnant women, a lack of financial resources was cited as the primary reason for
not seeking antenatal care in affected communities (Amoo et al., 2018). Orderud et al. (2022)
indicate that households affected by flooding often prioritize obtaining sufficient food and water,
leading to fewer resources available for recommended maternal healthcare, which may lead to
worse health outcomes.
Post-flood income has been identified as one of the main predictors of adequate access to
health services, demonstrating that families with higher post-disaster income are more likely
to obtain care, while those with lower incomes face significant barriers (Jacquet et al., 2016).
During the rainy season, declining household income often drives families to seek care from
lower-costtraditionalhealerswhooffercredit,buttheselesseffectivetreatmentscandelayformal
care and increase complications when patients eventually reach health facilities (Codjoe et al.,
2020).
Floods intensify poverty in ways that disproportionately harm women and children.
Families often withdraw children (especially girls) from school due to financial strain, increasing
risks of early marriage, teenage pregnancy, and child labour (Sadia et al., 2016). At the same
time, reliance on public health facilities that are frequently damaged or disrupted leaves most
families unable to access essential MCH services, further heightening vulnerability during and
after floods (Sadia et al., 2016).
The effects of floods on household income also affect nutrition. Baten et al. (2020)
highlight that floods make food both scarce and expensive, which then hurts household finances
and, over time, productivity. When income levels are stable (or can be supplemented by loans
and social networks, as discussed by Saulnier et al. (2020), households are more likely to secure
sufficient nutrition, which in turn helps preserve their health and work capacity.
3.3.3.2 Heatwaves
Evidence that heat exposure affects maternal health service use though income and
financial strain remains limited and indirect. In rural Nepal, Bishwakarma (2022) showed that
high temperatures are associated with reduced ANC use, likely operating through strained
household resources. In settings where households depend on agriculture and informal labour,
hot days increase the prices of key foods due to reduced yields for some crops and faster spoilage,
which gradually erodes purchasing power and constrain spending. This financial pressure may

115
lead women to delay or forgo preventive ANC, although the study does not directly observe
incomelossesordisentangletheseeffectsfrombroaderseasonalresponsestoheat(Bishwakarma,
2022).
Chenetal.(2022)highlightedarelated,butdownstream,mechanisminChina:exposureto
extremeheatlateinpregnancyincreasesnewbornhospitalizationcostsbynearly2%oftotalhealth
expenses. While this reflects higher expenditures rather than lost income, it similarly reduces
household financial capacity and exacerbates inequalities, with greater effects on less-educated
mothers.
3.3.4 Increased health risks (M4)
Mechanism 4, as illustrated in Figure 3.4, links to MCH utilisation through two main
routes that can operate at the same time: (i) demand shifts (more acute illness and complications
increase the need for care) and (ii) effective access falls (the health system and households have
less capacity to deliver or attend MCH services).

3.3.4.2 Heatwaves
Heat exposure during pregnancy may trigger physiological stress responses, such as
dehydration, reduced placental blood flow, and thermoregulatory strain, which can increase risks
of hypertensive disorders and preterm labor (Chen et al., 2022; Kim, Lee e Rossin-Slater, 2021).
These pathways lead to adverse birth outcomes including low birth weight, stillbirth, and preterm
delivery, which elevate neonatal intensive care use (Cil e Kim, 2022). During extreme heat
events, acute obstetric complications can escalate rapidly, driving greater demand for emergency
care (Quilty et al., 2024). As a result, heatwaves disrupt both routine and emergency maternity
services through increased admissions and visits, with socially vulnerable groups, including
Black women, disproportionately affected by these disruptions (Kim, Lee e Rossin-Slater, 2021).
Young children face health risks during extreme heat due to their immature thermoregula-
tory systems and higher fluid needs. Studies consistently show increases in pediatric emergency
visits during heatwaves, particularly among children under-5, driven by dehydration, respiratory
distress, heat illness, and infections (Campbell et al., 2019; Davis et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2016).
Heat exposure has also been linked to rises in intestinal infections, endocrine and metabolic
disorders, nervous system conditions, and chronic respiratory diseases among this age group,
reflectingcombinedeffectsofdehydration,bacterialgrowth,andthermalstressonmultipleorgan
systems (Xu et al., 2014). Xu et al. (2017) shows that infants’ hospital admissions only rose when
heatwaves were very intense (mean temperature≥97th percentile for≥2 days). The effect did not
differ by sex, indigenous status or neighbourhood socioeconomic level; indicating that all infants

117
are at risk.
Structural vulnerabilities in health facilities further intensify health risks associated with
heatwaves. Poor ventilation, unreliable power for cooling and vaccine storage, and overcrowded
wards create unsafe conditions and may compromise treatment quality (Codjoe et al., 2020). In
settings with widespread undernutrition, heat episodes additionally elevate the risk of neonatal
hyperthermia, as seen in India, where poor nutritional status reduces the body’s ability to cope
with thermal strain (Kakkad et al., 2014). Overall, heatwaves threaten children and pregnant
women through both direct physiological impacts and indirect disruptions to the quality and
safety of care environments.
3.3.5 Health service disruption (M5)
Mechanism 5, illustrated in Figure 3.5, captures how floods and heatwaves disrupt the
supply of health services by reducing the availability of health professionals and the operational
capacity of health facilities, thereby limiting the delivery of MCH services. Health service
disruption affects MCH service use by altering the feasibility and quality of care on the supply
side, not merely people’s need or willingness to seek services. Floods and heatwaves create a
supply shock through staff shortages, reduced functional space and equipment, and interrupted
supplies and referral pathways – often alongside a simultaneous surge in demand from injuries,
infections, dehydration, and pregnancy complications. Together, these pressures reduce routine
service provision and shift utilisation toward delayed or emergency care.

Floods also disrupt the availability and functionality of healthcare infrastructure. Health

and slow recovery timelines, increasing vulnerability to cascading failures when subsequent
events occur (Baten et al., 2020; Sadia et al., 2016).
These infrastructure and workforce disruptions are compounded by weakened system
coordination. Flooding reduces supervision of community health workers, undermining outreach
and continuity of care (Shah, Miller e Mothabbir, 2019). Limited public investment and poor
geographical targeting further contribute to chronically under-resourced services in flood-prone

Despite these challenges, some health systems demonstrate adaptive capacity. Social
networks and community-based responses can mitigate service disruption: in Cambodia and
Bangladesh, community volunteers facilitated emergency transport, supported communication,
and enabled health workers to reach patients despite flooding (Saulnier et al., 2022; Ray-Bennett
et al., 2021). Targeted deployment of midwives, supportive supervision, and restoration of
medical supplies have proven effective in maintaining outreach and rebuilding service continuity
in flood-affected settings (Purno et al., 2023).
Flooding often leads to significant logistical challenges that affect supply chains overall
and disrupt the delivery of medical supplies. Floods frequently disrupt power systems and supply
chains, rendering medical equipment such as emergency generators and vaccine refrigerators
inoperable. In facilities located in flood-prone areas, the loss of medications, supplies, and
equipment due to inundation is common (Codjoe et al., 2020). Supply chain interruptions
and delays in transporting pharmaceuticals contribute to stock-outs and further restrict service
provision (Wilunda et al., 2017; Chandir et al., 2023).

that healthcare infrastructure may be flooded or damaged, and medical supply deliveries can be
delayed.
3.3.5.2 Heatwaves
In low-resource settings, health workers often deliver care in overcrowded, poorly
ventilated environments where high indoor temperatures, power outages and compromised
refrigerationplacebothstaffandpatientsatrisk.InGhana,Codjoeetal.(2020)showthatextreme
heat causes health worker fatigue, increases infection risks during procedures and contributes to
delays in deliveries and outpatient care, while also interrupting vaccine and medicine cold chains.
Heatwaves also drive sharp surges in emergency care use among children. In Tasmania,
severe and extreme heatwaves increased paediatric ED visits for heatstroke and sunburn,
overwhelmingroutinecapacityandlimitingresponsivenesstootherurgentneeds(Campbelletal.,
2019). Similar patterns were observed in Roanoke, Virginia, where heatwaves “overtaxed” ED
systems, leading to crowding, poorer quality of care and increasing reliance on costly emergency
pathways (Davis et al., 2020).
Maternal care is similarly strained during extreme heat. In the United States, unplanned
emergency admissions for pregnancy complications rise on extremely hot days, increasing
workload for obstetric teams and reducing availability for scheduled care (Kim, Lee e Rossin-
Slater, 2021). In remote tropical regions such as northern Australia, extreme heat leads to more
emergency obstetric retrievals when health systems are already operating at capacity. This can
delay transfer of non-obstetric patients and place additional pressure on aeromedical teams and
tertiary hospitals (Quilty et al., 2024).
Importantly, some evidence indicates that targeted, context-specific adaptations can
mitigateheat-relatedrisksandeasepressureonhealthsystems.Inaresource-constrainedhospital
setting in India, relocating a maternity ward from an overheated upper floor to a cooler ground
level during a heatwave reduced neonatal intensive care admissions by 64%, demonstrating how
simple structural adjustments can lower neonatal risk and reduce staff burden under extreme heat
(Kakkad et al., 2014). More broadly, the literature suggests that anticipatory measures, such as
heatwave forecasting, surge staffing plans, and caregiver-focused prevention campaigns, may
help limit avoidable heat-related demand, although their effectiveness depends on local capacity,
infrastructure, and governance contexts (Campbell et al., 2019; Davis et al., 2020).
Extreme heat places substantial strain on health service infrastructure and delivery, with
particularly severe consequences in low-resource settings. In Ghana, poorly ventilated maternity

120
and primary care facilities have recorded indoor temperatures up to 6°C higher than outdoors,
while frequent power outages disrupt water supply, infection control, and vaccine refrigeration,
compromising the safety of deliveries and essential procedures and increasing staff fatigue;
together,thesefailuresinbasicinfrastructureunderminematernalandneonatalcareand,insome
cases, push patients toward costly private providers (Codjoe et al., 2020).
Similar pressures are observed in higher-income settings. During the 2013 heatwave in
England, rapid surges in health service use overwhelmed emergency and primary care, reducing
workforce productivity and straining energy systems that support equipment and cold-chain
reliability (Smith et al., 2016). Across contexts, extreme heat drives spikes in emergency visits
among children, overloading facilities and increasing dependence on energy-intensive cooling,
which heightens risks of power instability and supply chain disruption (Stowell et al., 2023).

3.3.6.1 Floods
Acrossflood-affectedsettings,theevidenceshowsthatdisruptionstogeneralinfrastructure
are sufficient to reduce effective MCH service utilisation even when facilities remain physically
intact. In Pakistan’s 2022 floods, Chandir et al. (2023) document a sharp and persistent decline in
immunization delivery in affected districts, with substantial shortfalls remaining months after
floodwaters receded despite intensive catch-up campaigns. This pattern is consistent with an
“operational foundations” mechanism: when routine outreach schedules, workforce deployment,
and local service organisation are disrupted at scale, services do not simply pause and rebound,
and missed care may not be fully recovered.

121
Evidence from Ghana (Codjoe et al., 2020) makes the energy and productivity path-
way explicit. Flooding disrupted electricity supply not only through facility-level damage but
because utilities pre-emptively disconnected power to prevent electrocution, while fuel supply
interruptions rendered generators unusable. These energy disruptions constrained refrigeration,
lighting, emergency procedures, and basic operations. At the same time, muddy and waterlogged
environments reduced staff mobility within and between facilities, increased time spent on
cleaning and recovery tasks, and diverted workforce effort away from routine care, directly
lowering productivity even without structural facility collapse.
Supply-chain fragility further amplifies these effects. In rural Bangladesh, Shah, Miller e
Mothabbir (2019) report increased stock-outs of essential commodities and reduced supervision
during flooding months, alongside an approximate 30% decline in child treatments delivered by
community providers. Their findings highlight how flooded transport routes interrupt medicine
distribution, delay resupply, and weaken supervisory and reporting systems. Similarly, Orderud
et al. (2022) synthesise evidence that floods damage transport and logistics networks, hinder
medical supply deliveries, and disrupt referral systems, even if average utilisation effects are
muted in chronically flood-prone areas where partial adaptation has occurred. In northern Iran,
Peyravi, Rahnavard e Marzaleh (2020) describe the immediate post-flood period as dominated by
logistical and coordination challenges, as the emergency health service continuity depends on
functioning distribution systems, communication networks, and energy supplies.
Finally, qualitative evidence from South Sudan (Wilunda et al., 2016; Wilunda et al.,
2017) shows that when roads are impassable for extended periods, referral and resupply systems
stall, forcing improvised solutions and placing additional physical burdens on communities and
health workers. This erosion of general infrastructure constrains utilisation and can generate both
immediate service declines and incomplete recovery over time.
3.3.6.2 Heatwaves
The available evidence linking heatwaves to disruptions in general infrastructure remains
limited and context-specific. In our review, the most detailed account comes from Ghana(Codjoe
et al., 2020).
In the Ghanaian context, Codjoe et al. (2020) describe how extreme heat increases
electricity demand for cooling, both in households and facilities, at the same time that national
power systems face structural fragilities. Ghana’s grid is characterized by periodic instability
due to generation constraints, transmission losses, reliance on hydropower sensitive to rainfall
variability, and limited reserve margins. During heat events, heightened demand for fans and air
conditioningcantriggervoltagefluctuations,localizedoutages,orloadshedding.Healthfacilities
dependent on prepaid electricity meters or diesel generators are particularly vulnerable: rising
fuel costs and supply constraints may force rationing of power to essential units, interrupting
lighting, refrigeration, and routine operations.
Heat also exposes weaknesses in temperature-sensitive supply chains. According to

122
Codjoe et al. (2020), vaccine refrigeration becomes unreliable when power outages coincide
with peak heat, as freezers struggle to maintain stable internal temperatures and ice packs fail to
refreeze adequately. Even where generators are available, fuel constraints limit continuous use.
These disruptions reflect vulnerabilities in upstream energy and logistics systems rather than
intrinsic failures of clinical care.
Finally, Codjoe et al. (2020) report that extreme heat reduces workforce productivity
both inside and outside health facilities. High temperatures impair sleep, increase fatigue, and
complicate clinical procedures due to excessive perspiration. Beyond the health sector, heat
reduces working hours in informal and manual labor markets, lowering household income and
constrainingspendingonhealthcare.Insettingswhereeconomicbuffersarethin,thisproductivity
loss may further weaken supply chains and service demand.
Overall, the evidence for an “operational stress” pathway under heatwaves is suggestive
rather than definitive. It is grounded primarily in the Ghanaian case, where power systems are
susceptible to demand surges and structural instability. While similar vulnerabilities likely exist
in other LMIC contexts with fragile grids and limited backup capacity, further comparative
research is needed to determine how broadly this mechanism applies to other settings.

3.4 DISCUSSION
A central contribution of this study is the development of a realist-informed Causal
Loop Diagram to synthesise and organise heterogeneous evidence on extreme weather events
and maternal and child health utilisation. By combining realist logic with systems thinking,
the review moves beyond linear cause–effect descriptions and instead maps how interacting
mechanisms generate reinforcing or dampening dynamics within health systems. This approach
aligns with broader calls in health systems research to adopt complexity-informed methods
capable of capturing feedback, spillovers, and unintended consequences (Adam e Savigny, 2012;
Cassidy et al., 2022).
The methodological positioning of this CLD is consistent with emerging guidance on
the use of CLDs in LMIC settings. Cassidy et al. (2022) emphasise that CLDs are particularly
valuable where primary data may be limited and where researchers seek to integrate multiple
forms of evidence (including systematic or realist reviews) into a coherent system representation.
Our ex-post development approach, grounded in secondary evidence synthesis, mirrors this
recommended pathway. However, as highlighted by Cassidy et al. (2022), validation through
stakeholder engagement remains critical. The present CLD therefore represents a theoretically
grounded synthesis rather than a fully validated system model.
Conceptually, our CLD also aligns with prior health sector CLDs that examine service
deliveryconstraints,immunisationuptake,andfinancingreformsinLMICs(Rwashana,Williams
e Neema, 2009; Paina e Peters, 2011; Cassidy et al., 2021). Similar to payment-for-performance
or immunisation CLDs, our model reveals reinforcing loops linking supply-side readiness,
demand-side income dynamics, and broader system foundations such as logistics and workforce
capacity. However, this study extends the literature by explicitly modelling climate shocks as
exogenous stressors that activate multiple loops simultaneously. While earlier CLDs often focus
on policy interventions internal to the health sector, our diagram embeds the health system
within energy systems, labour markets, transport networks, and climatic regimes. In doing so, it
contributes to a growing body of work applying systems thinking to health system resilience and
shock responsiveness (Ozawa, Paina e Qiu, 2016; Mudd et al., 2024).
One conceptual challenge concerns the treatment of context. Realist methodology treats
context as dynamically interacting with mechanisms, whereas CLDs often operationalise context
as an external boundary condition. In this study, contextual dimensions (population structure,
economic level, climate regime, and health system type) were not embedded as endogenous
variables but instead interpreted as conditions shaping which mechanisms activate and how
strongly.Thischoicepreservesdiagramclaritybutmayunderrepresenttheco-evolutionofcontext
and mechanism over time. Future modelling could endogenise selected contextual variables (e.g.,
adaptive capacity, infrastructure investment) to capture longer-term system transformation under

128
repeated shocks.
The synthesis reveals clear hazard-specific patterns. Flood studies (predominantly con-
ducted in low-income, tropical monsoon or savanna climates with mixed health systems) most
frequently activate mechanisms related to impaired mobility (M1), displacement (M2), income
loss (M3), and service strain (M5), often coupled with supply-chain or energy disruptions (M6).
The dominant outcome is reduced utilisation of routine MCH services. These patterns are
consistent with resilience frameworks that highlight infrastructure, logistics, and governance as
coredeterminantsofshockpropagationwithinhealthsystems(WorldHealthOrganization,2022).
In systems terms, floods appear to trigger reinforcing loops linking infrastructure breakdown,
income contraction, and service contraction.
In contrast, heatwave studies (largely from high-income and urban settings) tend to
activateclinicalriskpathways(M4)andoccasionallyoperationalstrain(M5),withoutcomesoften
characterisedbyincreasedemergencyutilisationratherthandecreasedroutinecare.Thissuggests
that heat may shift utilisation patterns toward acute episodes rather than uniformly suppressing
service access. The geographic distribution of this evidence also reflects data availability: high-
income settings more often capture emergency department visits, hospitalisations, and cost
outcomes. Importantly, climate regime and baseline adaptation capacity appear to condition
these effects, reinforcing the analytical value of incorporating Köppen–Geiger classifications and
system capacity variables.
The presence of null or maintained effects in a subset of flood studies further supports the
realist premise that outcomes depend on contextual activation. In settings with prior exposure,
established outreach systems, or rapid adaptive responses (e.g., mobile clinics, community boats,
temporary service reorganisation), shock-to-utilisation translation may be dampened. From a
systems perspective, these represent balancing loops that counteract reinforcing decline. Such
findingsresonatewithresilience-orientedCLDsthatemphasiseabsorptiveandadaptivecapacities
as buffers against cascading failure (Ozawa, Paina e Qiu, 2016).
Several limitations warrant consideration. First, the CLD is derived from secondary
evidence only; empirical validation through stakeholder engagement or group model-building,
as recommended by Cassidy et al. (2022), would strengthen causal confidence and contextual
specificity. Second, although contextual variation was systematically incorporated in the realist
synthesis, the diagram itself represents a generalised system architecture; regional adaptations
mayberequiredtoreflectdifferencesingovernancestructures,financingarrangements,orclimate
exposure. Third, leverage-point identification remains preliminary. Applying Meadows (1999)
hierarchy of leverage points could help distinguish shallow parameter changes (e.g., increasing
emergency supplies) from deeper structural interventions (e.g., redesigning information flows,
infrastructure standards, or system goals).
Finally, the CLD should not be interpreted as a predictive model. While many links
are empirically grounded, their relative strengths, time delays, and nonlinear thresholds remain
unquantified. Translating the diagram into a stock-and-flow simulation model would enable

129
estimationofloopdominance,explorationofsequentialorcompoundhazards,andassessmentof
policy scalability. Such integration of realist synthesis with quantitative system dynamics would
represent a next methodological frontier, deepening understanding of how climate-related shocks
propagate through maternal and child health systems.
3.5 CONCLUSION
Thisessayusedarealist-informedCLDtosynthesiseevidenceonthemechanismslinking
floods and heatwaves to MCH utilisation and to represent their interdependencies as a coherent
system. The resulting model suggests that utilisation losses are frequently driven by cascading
interactionsbetweenmobilityconstraints,householdeconomicshocks,anddisruptionstofacility
operations and supply chains, with reinforcing loops concentrated outside the health sector.
While the CLD offers a structured basis for identifying potential leverage points (especially
income buffering, transport continuity, and energy/logistics reliability) it remains an explanatory
synthesis rather than a predictive tool. Priority next steps include stakeholder validation and
quantitative system dynamics modelling to estimate loop dominance, time delays, and the likely
effectiveness of resilience policies under repeated and compound climate hazards.

4 FLOODS AND ANTENATAL CARE UTILISATION: EVIDENCE FROM NORTH-
EASTERN BRAZIL
ABSTRACT
Background:Gloods can disrupt maternal healthcare delivery through infrastructure
damage, access constraints, and health system strain. Yet little causal evidence exists on how
extreme floods affect routine antenatal care (ANC) utilisation in middle-income countries.
Methods:We examine the impact of the June 2010 floods in Pernambuco and Alagoas
on prenatal care utilisation using municipality-month panel data from 2008–2012. Municipalities
are classified as treated if officially affected by hydrological disasters during June 17–20, 2010,
and we implement strict exclusions to avoid contamination from other hydrological shocks
and potential spatial spillovers. Outcomes are municipality-level shares of live births by ANC
intensity (0, 1–3, 4–6, and≥7 visits) constructed from SINASC. We triangulate across two
quasi-experimental strategies: controlled interrupted time series (CITS), and modern event-study
difference-in-differences (DiD) estimators, while controlling for time-varying socioeconomic,
demographic, and health-system covariates and clustering standard errors at the municipality
level.
Results:Both CITS and event-study DiD estimates indicate a clear post-flood composi-
tional shift in ANC intensity. Flood exposure reduced the share of births preceded by≥7 ANC
visits and increased the share with 4–6 visits, with little evidence of effects on 0 visits or 1–3
visits. The CITS estimates show an immediate relative decline of about 6 percentage points in≥7
visits and an offsetting rise of roughly 4 percentage points in 4–6 visits at the intervention point,
with no meaningful differential post-flood slope changes. Aggregated event-study DiD estimates
are consistent with this pattern, indicating a statistically significant increase of 8.9 percentage
points in 4–6 visits and a decline of 10.5 percentage points in≥7 visits, while effects on 0 visits
and 1–3 visits are small and statistically non-significant. Dynamic estimates show no systematic
pre-trends and suggest persistent post-treatment differences over subsequent months.
Conclusion:TheJune2010floodsdidnotmeaningfullyincreasecompletenon-utilisation
of antenatal care, but they reduced the likelihood that women completed high-intensity ANC
schedules,shiftingutilisationfrom ≥7visitstowardintermediatecare(4–6visits).Thesefindings
suggest that in a high-coverage universal system, floods may primarily erode continuity and
schedule completion rather than eliminate contact with care. Climate-resilient health-system
policiesshouldthereforeprotectnotonlybasicaccessbutalsothecapacitytosustainrecommended
care trajectories during and after hydrological shocks.

4.1 INTRODUCTION
In June 2010, an extreme episode of heavy rainfall affected the northeastern region of
Brazil, producing widespread flooding across the states of Alagoas and Pernambuco. Torrential
rains over several days caused riverine overflow, infrastructure collapse (including bridges and
roads), and forced tens of thousands of people from their homes, with official reports noting
dozensoffatalitiesandemergencydeclarationsacrossmultiplemunicipalities(MouraeLandivar,
2010; Freire, Bonfim e Natenzon, 2014). Such hydrological disasters disrupt daily life, isolate
communities, and strain local public services, including primary healthcare facilities.
Floods represent the most common type of natural disaster worldwide, affecting approxi-
mately 102 million people each year, with higher incidence in developing countries and densely
populated urban areas (Freitas e Ximenes, 2012). In Brazil, hydrological disasters - that is, those
resulting in flooding and inundations - accounted for about one-third (5.568 occurrences, 34.9%)
of natural disasters between 2000 and 2015 (15.950 occurrences in total). However, in the same
period the average cost of hidrological disasters to healthcare facilities (R$ 599.411,75) was
proportionally higher than meteorological (R$ 292.416,43) and geological (R$ 199.228,61)
disasters (Freitas et al., 2020).
Prenatal services represent a cornerstone of maternal and child health systems worldwide,
offeringpreventivecare,riskscreening,andcontinuityofsupportthroughoutpregnancy.Antenatal
care (ANC) utilisation is widely considered not merely a measure of maternal health behaviours
but also a proxy for broader health service accessibility and functioning, particularly in settings
with universal or near-universal coverage.
At the international level, the WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION (2016) currently
recommends a minimum of eight contacts with antenatal care providers during pregnancy to
optimize maternal and perinatal outcomes and ensure a positive pregnancy experience. In Brazil,
complementarynationalguidelinesandpracticesemphasiseearlyinitiationofcareandcompletion

147
of an adequate number of visits, often operationalized locally as six or more consultations,
reflecting clinical priorities embedded in the Brazilian public health system (BRASIL, 2000).
Brazil’s Unified Health System (SUS) provides universal, publicly-funded healthcare,
with maternal and child health services delivered primarily at the municipal level through
primary health care networks (Padilha et al., 2025). The Family Health Strategy (Estratégia
Saúde da Família, FHS/ESF) is the principal model of primary care delivery, characterised by
multidisciplinary teams assigned to defined catchment populations. Prenatal care under SUS
is typically initiated and maintained within this primary care framework, with municipalities
exercising administrative autonomy while being supported by federal and state coordination
(Andrade et al., 2017). The decentralised structure of SUS implies that external shocks such
as floods operate at the local level and have the potential to disrupt routine service availability,
utilization patterns, and continuity of care.
Despite extensive research on the health impacts of disasters, the literature on how flood
events affect routine maternal health services remains limited, particularly in lower-middle-
income contexts (Chandra et al., 2025; Ummah, 2024; Orderud et al., 2022; Baten et al., 2020;
Haque, Parr e Muhidin, 2020a). Most existing studies on floods and maternal healthcare focus
on conditional probabilities of care or cross-sectional associations, and evidence using causal
inference frameworks is scarce. This gap is notable given that climate change is projected
to increase the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events globally, with significant
implications for health systems in LMICs.
This study aims to address this gap by investigating the causal effect of the June 2010
floodsonantenatalcareutilisationacrossmunicipalitiesinPernambucoandAlagoas,Brazil.Our
primary research question is:Did exposure to the June 2010 floods cause measurable changes
in antenatal care utilisation, and if so, how did the distribution of utilisation intensity shift
following the event?
To estimate these effects, we exploit a large municipality–month panel (2008–2012) and
use two complementary quasi-experimental identification strategies: (i) a controlled interrupted
time series analysis that contrasts pre- and post-shock trends between exposed and unexposed
municipalities; and (ii) modern event-study difference-in-differences estimators designed for
staggered treatment settings, which allow for dynamic measurement of impacts relative to the
timing of exposure. By combining these strategies, we aim to strengthen causal inference in a
setting where randomized experiments are infeasible and where conventional DiD approaches
face challenges related to treatment timing and panel imbalance.
Beyond this Introduction (Section 4.1), the remainder of the essay is structured as follows.
Section4.2outlinestheempiricalstrategy,explainingtherationaleforemployingbothacontrolled
interrupted time series design and a difference-in-differences approach. Section 4.3 presents the
main findings. Section 4.4 situates these results within the broader literature, drawing out their
policy implications and identifying directions for future research. Finally, Section 4.5 concludes
the essay.

4.2 METHODS
This section describes the data, outcome measures, and empirical strategies used to
estimate the effects of the June 2010 floods on prenatal care utilisation. After defining the
treated and control municipalities and the study variables, it presents two complementary
quasi-experimental approaches: a controlled interrupted time-series analysis and an event-study
difference-in-differences model. All statistical analyses were performed inR (version 4.4.2). For
transparency and replicability, all data processing and estimation scripts are made available in
the Appendix 4.A.
4.2.1 Data and measurement
In 2010, the study area consisted of 287 municipalities, of which 102 (35.54%) were
located in Alagoas and 185 (64.45%) in Pernambuco.
For this study, municipalities were classified as treated (n = 80; 27.87%) if they were
officially affected by any hydrological disasters - namely floods, heavy rainfall, flash floods,
inundations, or mass movements - between June 17 and 20, 2010. Treatment status was defined
based on official records from the Integrated Disaster Information System (S2iD), accessed
through the Brazilian Digital Atlas of Disasters.
Toconstructacrediblecontrolgroupandminimizeconfoundingeffects,severalexclusion
criteria were applied. First, municipalities affected by other hydrological disasters during the
study period (2008–2012) were excluded (n = 98; 34.15%), in order to avoid contamination of
the counterfactual by additional disaster shocks.
Second, municipalities not officially recorded as affected by the June 2010 floods but
geographically adjacent (queen contiguity) to treated municipalities were also excluded (n = 45;
15.68%). This exclusion aimed to account for potential spatial spillover effects and to mitigate
concerns regarding possible underreporting in the official disaster database - i.e., municipalities
that may have been affected but were not formally registered.
Finally, the municipality of Fernando de Noronha (n = 1; 0.35%) was also excluded
due to its insular geographic condition and markedly distinct socioeconomic and infrastructural
characteristics relative to mainland municipalities.
In total, 144 municipalities (50.18%) were excluded from the analysis. The remaining
municipalities (n = 63; 21.95%) constituted the control group.
We construct a municipality–month panel using SINASC microdata aggregated at the
municipality level, covering 60 monthly periods from January 2008 to December 2012. This
time window spans approximately five years around the June 2010 flood event, including roughly
two and a half years before and two and a half years after exposure.
The primary outcomes of interest are municipality-level shares of live births by number

multiparous mothers may reduce visits owing to prior experience or competing time constraints.

shares unrelated to flood exposure. The antenatal care determinants literature routinely identifies
parity as an important predisposing factor influencing utilisation (Morón-Duarte et al., 2021;
Aboagye et al., 2025; Wulandari, Laksono e Nantabah, 2020; Viellas et al., 2014).

may correlate with both vulnerability to disaster impacts and the ability to recover from shocks.

the importance of adjusting for compositional differences across municipalities (Morón-Duarte
et al., 2021; Leal et al., 2020; Anjos e Boing, 2016; Domingues et al., 2015; Viellas et al., 2014).

employ two complementary quasi-experimental strategies. A controlled interrupted time-series

difference-in-differences approach provides a more flexible assessment of dynamic treatment
effects and pre-intervention trends. Together, these methods allow us to evaluate both the timing
and persistence of changes across prenatal care intensity categories.

4.2.2.2 Event-study difference-in-differences
While the controlled interrupted time series (CITS) framework provides a flexible way to
estimate changes in levels and trends at the intervention cutoff, it imposes a parametric structure
on post-treatment dynamics. In particular, CITS restricts treatment effects to operate through
discrete level shifts and linear trend changes. However, disaster impacts may unfold nonlinearly
over time, with potentially heterogeneous short-, medium-, and longer-term responses.
Toallowforamoreflexibledynamicresponseandtoformallytestforpre-treatmentparallel
trends, we complement the CITS approach with an event-study difference-in-differences (DiD)
design. This framework estimates period-specific treatment effects relative to the intervention
month, without imposing linearity in post-treatment trends.

e Sant’Anna (2021), which generalizes the traditional two-way fixed effects DiD model and
provides consistent estimates under staggered or group-specific treatment timing. Although
treatment in our setting occurs at a single common time (July 2010), the Callaway e Sant’Anna
(2021)estimatorofferstwoimportantadvantages:(i)itavoidsbiasesassociatedwithconventional

To assess pre-intervention comparability between treated and control municipalities, we

commonly used in quasi-experimental designs to assess covariate balance.

Baseline comparisons reveal meaningful differences in levels between treated and control
municipalities. Treated areas exhibit a higher share of 7+ ANC visits and a lower share of 4–6

Importantly, difference-in-differences and controlled interrupted time series designs do

are included as controls in the DiD specifications, accounting for time-varying compositional

of prenatal care intensity and maternal characteristics, the empirical strategy exploits within-

prenatalcare.Instead,theyinducedanimmediatereallocationfromthehighest-intensitycategory
(7+ visits) toward intermediate utilisation (4–6 visits), with effects operating primarily through
level shifts at the intervention point rather than sustained changes in post-flood trends.
4.3.3 Difference-in-differences
This subsection presents the event-study difference-in-differences estimates of the effects
of the June 2010 floods on prenatal care utilisation. It first examines pre-treatment trends and the
evolution of effects over time, before reporting the aggregated average treatment effects for each
prenatal visit category. Figure 4.6 shows the dynamic estimates by month relative to the flood.

161
Figure 4.6 – Event Study Estimates
Overall, the event-study estimates support the parallel trends assumption and point to a
clear post-treatment reallocation across prenatal care intensity categories.
In the pre-treatment period (𝑡≤−1 ), coefficients for all outcomes fluctuate around zero
and are generally statistically indistinguishable from zero. This pattern is especially evident in
the 7+ visits and 4–6 visits panels, where there is no systematic upward or downward trend prior
to July 2010. The absence of pronounced pre-trends reinforces the credibility of the identifying
assumption.
After the shock (𝑡≥0 ), a marked divergence emerges between higher- and intermediate-
intensity care. The probability of receiving 7 or more visits declines persistently, with negative
point estimates increasing in magnitude roughly between three and twelve months post-treatment.
In contrast, the probability of receiving 4–6 visits rises over the same horizon, with positive
and gradually increasing coefficients. This divergence is clearly visible in the upper panels of
Figure 4.6 and is consistent with the aggregated ATT estimates.
For lower-intensity care, the effects are comparatively modest. Estimates for 1–3 visits
remain close to zero throughout most of the post-treatment period and do not display a consistent
dynamic pattern. Similarly, the probability of no visits exhibits small and imprecise fluctuations,
with confidence intervals generally encompassing zero.
Figure 4.6 suggests that the shock did not substantially increase complete exclusion from

prenatal care. Rather, it induced a shift away from the highest-intensity category (7+ visits)
towardintermediateutilisation(4–6visits).Thedynamicprofileindicatesagradualandpersistent
adjustment, rather than a short-lived disruption. Complete event-study estimates for the full
period are reported in Appendix 4.B.
