4.4 DISCUSSION
Thisstudyprovidesquasi-experimentalevidencethattheJune2010floodsinPernambuco
and Alagoas affected the intensity of antenatal care utilisation, rather than generating widespread
non-utilisation. Across both the controlled interrupted time series and the event-study DiD
estimates, we find a clear post-shock compositional shift: the share of births preceded by≥7
ANC visits declined, while the share with 4–6 visits increased, with no statistically meaningful
effects on 0 visits or 1–3 visits. These results are consistent with a partial disruption of care
continuity and/or scheduling regularity that reduced the probability of completing high-intensity
ANC, but did not substantially push women into complete exclusion from care.

163
International quantitative evidence generally suggests that flooding and related hazards
can depress maternal health-care utilisation, especially where shocks disrupt transport, facilities,
and household livelihoods. For example, studies in Bangladesh report lower odds of receiving
ANC from skilled providers and other MNH services in flood-affected areas, with stronger
negativeassociationswherefloodingisrecurrentratherthanepisodic(Batenetal.,2020;Orderud
etal.,2022).Relatedworklinkingdisplacementduetoextremeeventstomaternalcareutilisation
in rural Bangladesh finds that repeated displacement is associated with lower probabilities of
receiving ANC and of completing≥4 visits with a trained provider (Haque, Parr e Muhidin,
2020a). In India, recent analyses merging household survey data with flood-prone geographies
similarly report worse ANC adequacy or higher probability of incomplete ANC in flood-prone
districts, with particularly large disparities for socially marginalised groups (Barman et al., 2025;
Chandra et al., 2025).
At the same time, not all settings exhibit strong average effects once area characteristics
are accounted for. Evidence from Bangladesh using multi-survey data suggests that bivariate
associationsbetweenfloodingandmaternalserviceusecanattenuatesubstantiallyafteradjusting
for socioeconomic and demographic factors, implying that lower utilisation may partly reflect
structural disadvantages of flood-prone areas rather than the causal effect of flood events per se
(Orderud et al., 2022). Our findings sit between these two patterns. On one hand, we detect a
meaningful post-flood change that is consistent with disruption mechanisms emphasised in the
broader extreme-weather and maternal-health literature (Pappas, Kovats e Ranganathan, 2024;
Mallett e Etzel, 2018). On the other hand, the absence of effects at the lower tail (0 visits) is
consistent with the idea that, even under stress, some systems maintain a basic floor of access,
particularlywherebaselineANCcoverageishighandprimarycareisgeographicallywidespread.
A key substantive contribution of our results to this literature is what changes: rather than
a uniform decline in utilisation, the shock primarily reduced≥7visits and increased 4–6 visits.
This"downshifting"patternisoftennotobservableinstudiesthatfocusonlyonasingleadequacy
threshold (e.g.,≥4 visits) or binary outcomes. In practical terms, floods may not eliminate
ANC use in a high-coverage system, but they can impair the ability to complete recommended
schedules, potentially weakening the preventive, screening, and continuity functions of ANC.
The pattern we observe is also coherent with the broader determinants-of-ANC literature.
Frameworks of health services utilisation emphasise that care-seeking depends on (i) enabling
resources(income,transport,time),(ii)need/riskandperceivedneed,and(iii)supply-sideaccess
and quality (Andersen, 2008; Levesque, Harris e Russell, 2013). Flood shocks plausibly operate
through multiple channels simultaneously: damage to roads and bridges raises travel costs;
facility disruption and workforce displacement reduce appointment availability; and income
losses tighten household budgets and time constraints. These mechanisms predict reductions in
visit frequency even when some contact with the health system is maintained.
In Brazil, a large body of evidence documents persistent socioeconomic and geographic
gradients in ANC adequacy/quality, including strong associations with maternal education, age,

164
parity, and partnership status, as well as with broader regional and access barriers (Domingues
et al., 2015; Leal et al., 2020; Morón-Duarte et al., 2021; Anjos e Boing, 2016; Silva et al.,
2019). This context supports the interpretation that flood exposure may interact with pre-existing
disadvantages: municipalities with higher rurality, weaker transport connectivity, or more fragile
service networks may find it harder to sustain high-intensity ANC schedules during and after
a shock. In our setting, the finding that women did not move into non-utilisation on average is
consistent with Brazil’s near-universal ANC coverage reported in national surveys (Viellas et al.,
2014), but the redistribution away from≥7 visits is consistent with documented challenges in
ensuringadequateandhigh-qualitycareeveninnon-disasterperiods(Cunhaetal.,2019;Ortelan
et al., 2023; Esposti et al., 2020).
The CITS results suggest that the main effect operates through an immediate level shift
rather than a sustained divergence in trends, while the event-study DiD indicates a persistent
post-treatment difference over subsequent months. These two views are not contradictory. A
shock can generate an abrupt drop in high-frequency visits (missed appointments, cancelled
clinic days, interrupted follow-up), and then a new equilibrium may emerge as services "catch
up" partially but not fully restore pre-shock intensity. In settings where disruptions last beyond
the acute phase (because infrastructure repairs, rescheduling backlogs, and household recovery
take time) a level shift can remain visible over an extended horizon.
The international literature offers supportive parallels. Work relating precipitation anoma-
lies to disruptions in ANC provision in Malawi, for example, emphasises that climate-related
disruptioncanberecurrentandcumulativeratherthanashort-livedacuteinterruption,particularly
when transport and physical access are repeatedly compromised (Murray-Watson et al., 2025).
Similarly, evidence from floodplain settings shows that seasonal flooding can sharply reduce
geographic access to maternal services at particular times of year, indicating that even temporary
access barriers can meaningfully reshape utilisation patterns (Mroz et al., 2023).
The WHO climate-resilient health systems agenda emphasises strengthening core health-
system functions to manage climate risks, including service delivery, workforce, infrastructure,
information systems, financing, governance, and community engagement (World Health Orga-
nization, 2022). Interpreted through a resilience lens (absorptive, adaptive, and transformative
capacities), our results point to an important nuance: the maternal health-care system appears
to have absorbed the shock sufficiently to prevent large increases in complete non-use (0 ANC
visits), but did not fully preserve performance at the upper end of recommended contact. In the
language of resilience trajectories, this resembles a system that maintains an "acceptable" level
of functioning for most users (continued contact), while experiencing a measurable performance
drop in more resource-intensive or continuity-dependent components (completion of≥7 visits).
This distinction matters for policy. Absorptive capacity may reflect the existence of a
broad primary-care network, continuity mechanisms, and baseline high coverage that can keep
some ANC functioning even when infrastructure is stressed. Adaptive capacity may involve
reorganisationofcarepathways,outreach,prioritisationofhigher-riskpregnancies,andtemporary

165
alternatives(e.g.,rebooking,redistributionofstaff,ormobilecare),whichcansustainintermediate
levels of ANC but may not fully restore high-frequency schedules immediately. Qualitative
evidence from flood contexts highlights precisely these adaptive strategies (reorganising flows,
itinerantcare,andcoordinationacrosslevels)askeytomaintainingmaternalcareduringflooding
(Saulnier et al., 2022; Nunes et al., 2025). From this perspective, our "downshifting" pattern may
represent an adaptive prioritisation under constraint: ensuring a minimum package of visits for
many women, at the cost of fewer women completing the highest-intensity schedules.
This study contributes to the floods–maternal health literature in three ways. First, it
provides causal, event-study DiD evidence in a large municipality–month panel around a well-
definedextremeevent,usingestimatorsdesignedforstaggered-treatmentandmodernDiDsettings
(Callaway e Sant’Anna, 2021). Second, it distinguishes impacts across the full distribution of
ANCintensity(0,1–3,4–6, ≥7 ),showingthatshocksmayreallocateutilisationacrosscategories
rather than simply reduce use on average. Third, by combining CITS and event-study DiD
evidence,itoffersconvergentvalidity:bothapproachesindicatethatthekeyeffectisareallocation
from high-intensity to intermediate-intensity care.
Several limitations should be considered. First, treatment status relies on official disaster
records; misclassification (underreporting or heterogeneity in severity within municipalities)
could attenuate estimated effects. Second, outcomes are municipality-level shares based on
live births; while this design captures population-level patterns, it cannot separate behavioural
changes from compositional shifts in who becomes pregnant or carries to term after the shock.
Third, we do not observe the content or quality of ANC visits, only visit counts/categories;
a stable number of visits does not necessarily imply stable quality. Fourth, despite excluding
adjacent municipalities and other hydrological disasters to reduce contamination, some spillovers
(e.g., cross-municipality service substitution) may persist and would typically bias estimates
toward zero. Finally, external validity is bounded: the SUS context, baseline ANC coverage, and
the institutional footprint of primary care in Northeast Brazil may differ from lower-coverage
systems where floods can plausibly generate stronger effects on complete non-use.
The results suggest that flood preparedness and response policies should not focus solely
on preventing complete care interruption, but also on protecting continuity and the ability
to complete recommended ANC schedules. In practice, this points to resilience investments
aligned with WHO’s climate-resilient health systems framework (World Health Organization,
2022): safeguarding facility functionality and transport connectivity, surge staffing and flexible
scheduling, robust information systems for tracing missed appointments, and proactive outreach
for pregnant women in affected areas. Future work should examine heterogeneity (e.g., by
baseline rurality, poverty, or health-system capacity), incorporate severity measures of flood
exposure, and, where possible, link utilisation shifts to maternal and neonatal outcomes to
quantify welfare-relevant consequences of the observed "downshifting" in ANC intensity.

166
4.5 CONCLUSION
Usingmunicipality–monthpaneldatafrom2008–2012andtriangulatingacrosscontrolled
interrupted time series and modern event-study difference-in-differences estimators, we find
that the June 2010 floods in Pernambuco and Alagoas causally altered the intensity of antenatal
care utilisation rather than producing widespread non-use. Flood exposure generated a clear
redistributionfromhigh-intensitycare( ≥7visits)towardintermediateutilisation(4–6visits),with
no statistically meaningful changes in the shares receiving 0 visits or only 1–3 visits. Interpreted
through a health-systems resilience lens, these results suggest that SUS and local primary
care networks largely preserved a floor of access during the shock, but struggled to maintain
continuityandschedulecompletionattheupperendofrecommendedcare.Policyeffortstobuild
climate-resilient maternal health services should therefore prioritise mechanisms that sustain
continuitysothatextremefloodsdonottranslateintosystematicshortfallsinrecommendedANC

5 CONCLUSION
This thesis investigated how extreme weather events (with emphasis on floods and
heatwaves) affects the utilization of maternal and child health (MCH) services. From a health
economics perspective and grounded in an understanding of health systems as complex adaptive
systems,theoverarchingobjectivewastogenerateintegratedevidenceona)whethertheseevents
alter the utilization of essential services (antenatal, delivery, postnatal, and child health care), b)
through which mechanisms such changes occur, and c) in which contexts these effects tend to be
amplified, with direct implications for public policies on adaptation, resilience, and equity in
access.
The common thread connecting the three essays is the proposition that extreme climate
events should not be treated as isolated shocks, but rather as systemic disruptions that propagate
simultaneously through both demand- and supply-side channels of health services. In economic
terms, floods and heatwaves alter access costs (time, transportation, risk), household budget
constraints(incomeloss,displacement),andtheproductionconditionsofservices(infrastructure,
workforce,logistics,andservicecapacity).Thisunifyingperspectivehelpsexplainwhy,incertain
contexts,thesystem’sresponseisnotasimple“collapse”inutilization,butratherareorganization
in the form and intensity of care use, often reproducing or deepening pre-existing vulnerabilities.
The original contributions of the thesis stem from the methodological complementarity
acrosstheessays.Essay1,arealist-informedsystematicreview,organizedafragmentedliterature
and showed that floods tend to more consistently compromise routine services (antenatal care,
institutionaldelivery,andpostnatalcare),whereasheatwavesaremorefrequentlyassociatedwith
increased acute and hospital-based utilization, although important gaps remain regarding their
effects on the continuity of routine care. By explicitly identifying Context–Mechanism–Outcome
configurations, the essay demonstrated that impacts are not uniform; rather, they depend on
socioeconomic vulnerability, rurality, infrastructure, response capacity, and the institutional
design of the health system.
Essay 2translated these findings into an integrated explanatory framework through a
Causal Loop Diagram (CLD), representing MCH service utilization as the result of dynamic
interactionsamongmobility,displacement,income,healthrisks,serviceprovision,anddisruptions
to infrastructure and supply chains. The CLD highlights that a significant share of vulnerability
in maternal and child care originates outside the health sector, in domains such as transportation,
energy, labor markets, and social protection. At the same time, by mapping reinforcing and
balancing feedback loops, the essay shows how climate shocks can generate persistent effects (for
example, through income loss and deterioration of local capacity), or be dampened by adaptive
mechanisms(servicereorganization,outreach,mobilecare,inter-municipalcoordination),thereby
identifying leverage points for resilience-oriented policies.
Essay 3provided novel causal evidence directly applicable to the Brazilian context by

200
estimating the effect of the 2010 floods in Pernambuco and Alagoas on antenatal care utilization,
using administrative data and a robust inference strategy (controlled interrupted time series and
event-study difference-in-differences). The main finding was that the shock did not, on average,
produce a substantial increase in exclusion from antenatal care (zero visits), but rather generated
a reallocation in the intensity of care: a reduction in the proportion of women with seven or more
visitsandanincreaseintheintermediatecategory(4–6visits).Intermsofsystemfunctioning,this
pattern suggests a partial disruption in continuity and in the capacity to complete recommended
care trajectories, rather than a total breakdown of access. It is a particularly relevant finding in
high-coverage systems such as Brazil’s Unified Health System (SUS), where maintaining some
contact may be more likely than preserving the ideal intensity of follow-up.
Taken together, the results of the thesis support a central implication: climate adaptation
policiesinhealthshouldnotfocussolelyontheminimalgoalof“avoidingcompleteinterruption”,
butalsoonprotectinglessvisibleandequallycriticaldimensionsofcareperformance:continuity,
adherencetorecommendedschedules,recoverycapacity,andequity.Inpracticalterms,thispoints
to actions aligned with the agenda of climate-resilient health systems, including: a) strengthening
infrastructure and connectivity (safe routes, bridges, patient transport, contingency planning); b)
enhancingresponsecapacityinprimarycareandmaternal–childnetworks(reserveteams,flexible
scheduling, rapid rebooking of missed appointments, network coordination); c) developing
information systems capable of tracking missed visits and recontacting pregnant women after
events; d) ensuring resilient logistics and supplies (energy, essential inputs, communication); and
e) integrating health policy with social protection and territorial management strategies, given
the roleof income,displacement, and mobilityin shapingutilization. From anequity perspective,
the thesis reinforces that climate shocks tend to exacerbate pre-existing disadvantages; therefore,
adaptation strategies must be explicitly designed to prioritize the most vulnerable groups and
localities with lower absorptive and adaptive capacity.
Despite its contributions, important research challenges and opportunities remain. Key
avenues for future work include: a) advancing the measurement of event intensity and severity
(beyond binary classifications), incorporating flood depth, duration, economic losses, and
infrastructure failures; b) exploring heterogeneity by socioeconomic vulnerability, rurality,
system capacity, and baseline coverage to identify where “downshifting” in care intensity is most
likely and most harmful; c) linking utilization changes to maternal and neonatal outcomes in
order to quantify welfare consequences and avoidable costs associated with partial disruptions in
continuity; d) expanding evidence on heatwaves and routine maternal–child care (not only acute
use), particularly in LMICs and underrepresented regions; and e) transforming the CLD into a
quantitative system dynamics model (stocks and flows) validated with stakeholders, enabling
simulation of scenarios, delays, cumulative effects, and policies under compound and recurrent
climate risks.
In sum, this thesis demonstrates that extreme climate events affect maternal and child
health not only through direct clinical risks, but through disruptions that cut across local

201
economies and service organization, altering utilization patterns and threatening continuity of
care. By combining realist evidence synthesis, mechanism-based systems modeling, and causal
inference applied to Brazil, the research offers an integrated contribution to health economics
and to the climate adaptation agenda: strengthening resilience requires not only maintaining
access, but also preserving care trajectories, especially for those already living at the margins of
the system. In a context of intensifying climate extremes, safeguarding the continuity and equity
of maternal and child health care is both a public health priority and a strategic investment in
long-term well-being and human capital.
